questions.title: Why Terraform Diffs Against State, Not the Live Cloud
questions.prompt: A junior engineer on your team manually resized a VM in the Azure Portal last week. To save time today, they ran `terraform plan -refresh=false` and it reported no changes at all, even though they know the real VM size no longer matches what's declared in the .tf config. Explain exactly what `terraform plan` normally diffs against, what `-refresh=false` changes about that, why drift like this usually does get caught, and why losing or corrupting the state file entirely is uniquely dangerous given how this diff mechanism actually works.
questions.modelAnswer:
Terraform's plan and apply fundamentally diff your .tf configuration against the STATE file -- not directly against whatever's actually running in the cloud right now. State is Terraform's own memory of what it created and what it looked like the last time Terraform checked, recorded with every resource's ID and attributes.

Normally, plan also performs a refresh as its first step: it queries each managed resource's real attributes from the provider's API and updates its in-memory copy of state before computing the diff. That refresh is exactly why a hand-made change like this VM resize usually does get caught -- the refreshed state picks up the new size, compares it against the unchanged .tf config, and shows a correcting diff.

`-refresh=false` skips that step entirely. Terraform computes the diff purely against whatever state already says on disk, without re-checking the provider first. Since nobody told Terraform about the manual resize, state still records the old size -- and since nobody updated the .tf file either, config still declares the old size too. Config matches state perfectly, so the diff is zero, even though neither of them matches the real VM anymore. This isn't a bug; it's `-refresh=false` doing precisely what it says, suppressing the one step that would have surfaced the drift.

This also explains why losing the state file is catastrophic under this mechanism: state is Terraform's only record of ownership and last-known values. With it gone, the next plan has nothing to diff against except an assumption of zero existing resources, so Terraform concludes everything declared in config needs to be created from scratch -- against infrastructure that's still very much alive and running.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk them through the one fact that explains almost everything confusing about Terraform: plan never actually looks at the live cloud directly to decide what to do -- it looks at state, and state is just Terraform's memory of what it did last time. Normally plan refreshes that memory first by actually calling out to Azure, which is why a manual change usually does show up as a diff. But they ran with `-refresh=false`, which skips that call entirely, so Terraform is comparing the .tf file against stale state -- and since neither one ever learned about the manual resize, they agree with each other and disagree with reality. It's not broken, it's just not looking where they assumed it was looking. And I'd use the moment to flag the scarier implication -- if that state file ever got deleted or corrupted, Terraform wouldn't have a 'that already exists, go check it' fallback. It would just assume zero resources exist and try to create everything in config from scratch, which against real running infrastructure is exactly the wrong thing to happen.
commonMistakes: Assuming terraform plan always reflects the true live state of a resource, regardless of flags
Not knowing that plan performs a refresh step by default before computing its diff
Treating '-refresh=false' as purely a performance flag with no correctness implications
Believing a resource's state entry is updated just by someone looking at or running plan on it
Underestimating how dangerous state loss is because they think Terraform could just 're-check the cloud'
keyPoints: Terraform diffs .tf configuration against the state file, not directly against the live cloud
Plan normally refreshes state from the provider API as its first step
-refresh=false skips that refresh, so the diff runs against stale state
If state and config agree (even if both are stale), plan reports zero changes
Losing the state file removes Terraform's only record of ownership, causing a 'recreate everything' plan

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains plan diffs config against state, not live cloud
Correctly explains the refresh step and what -refresh=false disables
Explains why config and state can agree while both are wrong
Connects this mechanism to why state loss is uniquely dangerous
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Wiring S3 Remote State with DynamoDB Locking from Scratch
questions.prompt: You're setting up a brand-new AWS-hosted Terraform project for a team of six. Write the backend configuration and the one-time bootstrap resource needed so that (a) state lives in a shared, versioned S3 bucket instead of anyone's laptop, and (b) two people running `apply` within the same minute can't corrupt that state. Then explain why the DynamoDB table needs exactly the schema it does, and why it can't be created inside the same configuration it's going to protect.
questions.modelAnswer:
Two separate pieces are needed, and they have to be bootstrapped in a specific order.

First, the backend block for the real project, pointing at a versioned S3 bucket plus a DynamoDB table for locking:

```hcl
terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket         = "acme-terraform-state"
    key            = "app-prod/terraform.tfstate"
    region         = "us-east-1"
    dynamodb_table = "terraform-locks"
  }
}
```

`bucket` and `region` identify the S3 bucket (created ahead of time, ideally with versioning enabled so an overwritten state can be recovered); `key` is this project's object path inside it, which is what lets one bucket safely hold many projects' state side by side; `dynamodb_table` is the piece that actually makes concurrent applies safe.

That table needs exactly one thing: a primary key named `LockID`, of type String -- Terraform writes and deletes a row keyed on the state file's path to claim and release the lock. It has to be provisioned in a *separate*, earlier bootstrap configuration, not the project config that will use it as its backend, because of a chicken-and-egg problem: the project's own state can't be stored in a backend whose supporting lock table doesn't exist yet. The bootstrap config runs with local (or an already-existing) state, creates the table once, and only then does the real project's backend block reference it.

```hcl
# bootstrap/main.tf -- run once, with its own (local or separate) state
resource "aws_dynamodb_table" "terraform_locks" {
  name         = "terraform-locks"
  billing_mode = "PAY_PER_REQUEST"
  hash_key     = "LockID"

  attribute {
    name = "LockID"
    type = "S"
  }
}
```

For contrast: the `azurerm` backend needs none of this -- it locks automatically using Azure Blob Storage's native lease mechanism, with no extra argument or resource at all.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd set this up in two steps, in a specific order, because there's a real chicken-and-egg problem if you don't. First I'd bootstrap a tiny standalone config -- its own state, nothing fancy -- that just creates the S3 bucket with versioning on, and a DynamoDB table called something like terraform-locks with a String primary key named exactly LockID, because that's the only schema Terraform's s3 backend actually knows how to use. That table has to exist before the real project can reference it, so it can't live in the same state it's protecting -- you'd be trying to use a backend that depends on a resource that isn't created yet. Once that's up, the real project's backend block is simple: bucket, key, region, and dynamodb_table pointing at that table. And I'd always flag the asymmetry to the team -- if we were on Azure instead, none of this DynamoDB step would exist, because the azurerm backend gets locking for free from blob storage's native lease feature. S3 just doesn't have an equivalent, so Terraform leans on DynamoDB to fill that gap.
commonMistakes: Forgetting the dynamodb_table argument entirely, so remote state exists but concurrent applies still aren't protected
Using the wrong primary key name or type on the table (it must be exactly LockID, type String)
Trying to create the DynamoDB table in the same configuration/state that will use it as its backend
Not enabling S3 bucket versioning, losing the ability to recover an overwritten state
Assuming the azurerm backend needs the same DynamoDB-style setup when it locks automatically via blob lease
keyPoints: s3 backend requires bucket, key, and region at minimum
Locking on s3 requires a separate dynamodb_table argument
The lock table's schema must be a String primary key named LockID
The lock table must be bootstrapped outside the configuration it protects
azurerm backend locks automatically via native blob lease, with no equivalent setup

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct backend "s3" block syntax with dynamodb_table
Correct DynamoDB table schema (LockID, String)
Explains why the table must be bootstrapped separately
Contrasts with azurerm's automatic locking
Mentions bucket versioning for durability
Overall clarity and correctness

questions.title: Pinning a Module Two Different Ways
questions.prompt: Your platform team publishes a reusable `network` module. One internal project consumes it straight from a Git repository (no registry involved); another consumes the exact same module from your organization's Terraform Cloud private module registry. Write the two `module` blocks, pinned so neither project picks up an unreviewed change automatically, and explain why the same `version` argument that works for one source does nothing at all for the other.
questions.modelAnswer:
Registry-sourced module -- the `version` argument works here because Terraform resolves it against the registry protocol, the same constraint syntax providers use:

```hcl
module "network" {
  source  = "app.terraform.io/acme/network/azurerm"
  version = "~> 1.2"
}
```

`source` is a registry address (`<host>/<org>/<name>/<provider>`), not a file path. `version = "~> 1.2"` constrains Terraform to the 1.2.x release line, so a `2.0` with breaking changes can't get pulled in by a plain `terraform init -upgrade`.

Git-sourced module -- here `version` does nothing, because there's no registry protocol resolving it. The pin instead lives in the source URL itself, as a `?ref=` query parameter:

```hcl
module "network" {
  source = "git::https://github.com/acme/terraform-modules.git//network?ref=v1.2.0"
}
```

`git::` tells Terraform this is a git repository rather than a plain download; the double slash before `network` points at a subdirectory, useful when one repo holds several modules; `?ref=v1.2.0` is the actual pin -- a tag, branch, or commit SHA. Moving to `v1.3.0` means editing that string and running `terraform init -upgrade`, exactly the same deliberate act that bumping `version = "~> 1.3"` would be for the registry source.

The reason `version` is a no-op for the git source: it's an argument Terraform's registry-resolution logic interprets, and a `git::` source never goes through that resolution path at all -- the source string, including whatever ref it carries, *is* the entire version identity for that kind of source.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write both and then make sure the team understands why they're not interchangeable. For the registry one, `version` does real work -- Terraform treats it like a provider constraint and won't silently jump to a 2.0 release. For the git one, I'd point out that `version` is just... ignored. It's not an error, it doesn't even warn you, it just does nothing, because Terraform never runs registry resolution logic against a raw git source in the first place. The actual pin for a git module lives right in the source string, as a `?ref=` tag or commit. I've seen people put `version = "~> 1.2"` on a git-sourced module block, feel like they've pinned it, and then get surprised months later when the module's default branch moved out from under them -- that's exactly the gap I'd want to close before it bites someone.
commonMistakes: Putting version on a git-sourced module, expecting it to pin anything
Forgetting the ?ref= query parameter, which tracks the default branch instead of a fixed point
Omitting the git:: prefix, causing Terraform to misinterpret the source string
Forgetting the double-slash before the subdirectory path in a multi-module repository
Not running terraform init -upgrade after bumping either pin, so the old version keeps being used
keyPoints: version only applies to registry-protocol module sources
Git sources pin via a ?ref= parameter appended to the source URL itself
git:: prefix plus // subdirectory syntax for multi-module repos
A private module registry is consumed identically to the public one, just with the org's host
terraform init -upgrade is required to actually move to a new pin either way

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct registry module block with version constraint
Correct git module block with ?ref= pin
Explains why version is a no-op for git sources
Explains terraform init -upgrade's role in moving to a new pin
Notes private registry behaves like the public one
Clarity

questions.title: Diagnosing a Subnet Error That's Really a Deleted NSG
questions.prompt: Your prod Terraform plan suddenly fails with the error shown below. Nobody touched the Terraform config this week. Walk through how you'd diagnose what actually happened, the exact first command you'd run before changing anything, and the two different fixes depending on what you find -- and why those two fixes use completely different Terraform commands.
questions.code: Error: updating Subnet "snet-cra-prod-0" (Virtual Network "vnet-cra-prod" / Resource Group "rg-cra-prod-network"): network.SubnetsClient#CreateOrUpdate: ... NetworkSecurityGroupNotFound: Resource ... "nsg-cra-prod-web" ... could not be found.
questions.modelAnswer:
That error is thrown against the subnet association, not plainly against the NSG itself, which is exactly why it feels confusing -- nothing in the message says "someone deleted your NSG," it takes a careful read to connect NetworkSecurityGroupNotFound back to a resource Terraform's state still insists exists. The likely cause is someone deleting `nsg-cra-prod-web` by hand in the Azure Portal, convinced it was orphaned.

Before touching anything, the first command is a state backup: `terraform state pull > prod-backup-2026-10-28.tfstate`. The remote backend already keeps blob versions, but that's a safety net for the backend, not a substitute for having a known-good local copy in hand before any state-modifying command -- state surgery is unforgiving, and a wrong resource address can silently drop something Terraform still needs to track.

Next, read what Terraform believes exists: `terraform state list | grep network_security_group` shows both the NSG resource and the subnet association still tracked, pointing at an NSG that no longer exists in Azure. That's the moment to figure out which of two real situations applies.

Path A -- nothing replaced it: the state entries are simply stale. `terraform state rm` on both the association and the NSG removes them from Terraform's bookkeeping without touching anything in Azure (state rm never deletes real infrastructure). `terraform plan` then shows a clean pair of creates, and `apply` rebuilds both exactly as code already defines.

Path B -- someone already recreated an NSG with the same name by hand: running `apply` without fixing state first would try to create a duplicate and fail with an "already exists" error, or worse, silently diverge. The right move is `terraform import` to adopt the existing object into state instead of recreating it, followed immediately by `terraform plan` to see exactly where the hand-made rules drifted from what the code expects, so that gets reconciled deliberately instead of guessed at.

The two fixes use different commands because they're solving different problems: `state rm` is for an entry that's now wrong and should simply stop being tracked; `import` is for a real object that exists and needs to start being tracked without being recreated.
questions.professionalAnswer: If this landed on my desk, the first thing I'd do is actually read what the error is complaining about -- it says NetworkSecurityGroupNotFound, attached to the subnet association, not plainly 'your NSG is gone,' so I wouldn't go chasing the NSG resource block itself first. Before I touch anything, I pull a state backup -- terraform state pull to a local file -- because once you start editing state, you want a way back if you get an address wrong. Then I'd run state list filtered to network security group and see both the NSG and the association still sitting in state. From there it's really just one question: did anything replace that NSG, or is it just gone? If nothing replaced it, state rm on both entries cleans up the stale tracking -- doesn't touch Azure at all -- and the next plan just wants to recreate them cleanly. If someone already rebuilt an NSG with the same name by hand, I'd import it instead of letting apply try to create a duplicate, and I'd run plan right after to see exactly where the hand-made version drifted from what the code expects.
questions.example:
terraform state pull > prod-backup-2026-10-28.tfstate
terraform state list | grep network_security_group

# Path A: nothing replaced it
terraform state rm azurerm_subnet_network_security_group_association.prod_web
terraform state rm azurerm_network_security_group.prod_web

# Path B: someone already recreated it by hand
terraform import azurerm_network_security_group.prod_web \
  /subscriptions/<sub-id>/resourceGroups/rg-cra-prod-network/providers/Microsoft.Network/networkSecurityGroups/nsg-cra-prod-web
terraform plan
commonMistakes: Skipping the state backup before running any state-modifying command
Assuming terraform state rm deletes the real Azure resource (it never does)
Running terraform apply blindly without first checking state list to know which path applies
Using import without immediately running plan afterward to catch divergence in hand-made rules
Chasing the NSG as the error's subject when the error actually surfaces against the dependent association
keyPoints: The error surfaces against the dependent resource, not necessarily the deleted one
terraform state pull backup is the mandatory first step before any state surgery
terraform state list shows exactly what Terraform currently tracks
state rm is for stale entries nothing replaced; import is for a hand-recreated real object
plan immediately after import verifies and surfaces any drift in the recreated object

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses why the error points at the association, not the NSG
Names state pull backup as the mandatory first step
Correctly distinguishes the two scenarios and matching fix
Correctly explains state rm/import never touch real infra (except import's read)
Mentions plan-after-import as the verification step

questions.title: The Import That Terraform Wants to Undo
questions.prompt: A teammate ran `terraform import aws_s3_bucket.data acme-data-bucket` successfully to bring a years-old bucket under management, reported the import as 'done,' and moved on. The next CI run's `terraform plan` shows `# aws_s3_bucket.data will be destroyed (because aws_s3_bucket.data is not in configuration)`. Explain exactly why that happened, what `terraform import` does and doesn't do that makes this possible, and the correct full workflow your teammate should have followed instead.
questions.modelAnswer:
`terraform import` only ever writes to state. It reads the real resource from the provider's API and records it in `terraform.tfstate` -- it never creates, modifies, or destroys anything in the real world, and critically, it does not write a matching `.tf` resource block for you by default. The teammate ran the import, it succeeded at the one thing it does (linking an address to a real resource ID in state), and stopped there.

The next `terraform plan` compares config against state the way it always does. State now has a tracked `aws_s3_bucket.data`, but config has no resource block declaring it. Terraform concludes, correctly and by design, that the resource is no longer wanted and proposes destroying it -- this isn't a bug, it's ordinary reconciliation finding a resource present in one side and absent from the other.

The correct workflow writes the resource block first (or at least before considering the job done): declare `resource "aws_s3_bucket" "data" { ... }` with your best understanding of its real attributes, run the import to link that address to the real bucket, then run `terraform plan` and actually read the diff. If plan shows changes, that means the resource block's arguments don't yet match the real object's values -- the fix is editing the config to match reality, not the other way around, until plan reports zero changes. Only then is the resource genuinely, safely under management. Terraform 1.5+ also offers `terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf` after an `import` block, which writes a best-guess starting resource block from the real object's attributes for you to review rather than typing from scratch.
questions.professionalAnswer: Honestly, this is one of those things that trips people up because 'import' sounds like it should do more than it does. All it actually did was write one entry into state -- it never touched the real bucket, and it definitely didn't write a .tf file for your teammate. So the next plan looks at config, sees nothing declaring that bucket, looks at state, sees it's tracked, and does exactly what it's supposed to do: proposes destroying something it thinks is no longer wanted. It's not being dramatic, it's just reconciling honestly. The fix is just doing the steps in the right order -- write the resource block first, run import to link it to the real bucket, and then actually read the plan output. If plan shows changes, that's telling you the block doesn't match reality yet, so you adjust the config, not the resource, until plan says nothing's different. Only then is it really 'done.' I'd also mention the newer generate-config-out flag, since it saves you guessing at the starting block by hand.
commonMistakes: Treating 'import succeeded' as 'done' without ever adding the matching resource block
Not running plan immediately after import to verify the config matches reality
Assuming import writes HCL for you by default
Editing the resource block blindly to match whatever plan shows, without understanding the underlying mismatch
Assuming this orphaned-state problem is specific to S3 rather than true of every resource type
keyPoints: import only writes to state; it never touches real infrastructure and doesn't generate HCL by default
Correct order is: write the resource block, import, plan, reconcile
A resource present in state with nothing in config is marked for destruction by design, not a bug
plan must show zero changes before the import is considered complete
-generate-config-out is an optional accelerant for writing the starting resource block

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains import only writes to state
Correctly diagnoses the destroy-plan as an orphaned state entry
Gives the correct full workflow in the right order
Mentions -generate-config-out or an equivalent verification step
Clarity

questions.title: Reading a State Lock Error Correctly
questions.prompt: Your `terraform apply` fails immediately with the error shown below. A teammate on Slack suggests just running `terraform force-unlock` so you can proceed. Is that the right call here? Walk through exactly what this error is telling you, what you should check before doing anything, and when force-unlock actually is appropriate.
questions.code:
Error: Error acquiring the state lock

Lock Info:
  ID:        5f8c1e2a-9b3d-4a7e-8c1f-2d6e0a44b912
  Path:      app-prod/terraform.tfstate
  Operation: OperationTypeApply
  Who:       alice@acme-laptop
  Version:   1.9.5
  Created:   2026-10-20 14:32:07 UTC
questions.modelAnswer:
No, force-unlocking on a Slack suggestion alone is the wrong call here. State locking exists precisely because a remote backend by itself doesn't stop two people from writing to state at the same time; before writing, Terraform acquires an exclusive lock, and any other apply or plan that needs to write has to wait. This error means another apply already holds that lock.

The message itself is directly useful and should be read, not skipped past: it names who holds the lock (`alice@acme-laptop`), what operation they're running (`OperationTypeApply`), and when it started. The right first move is almost always to check with Alice -- is her apply actually still running? -- and simply wait for it to finish, which releases the lock automatically.

`terraform force-unlock <LOCK_ID>` exists for the genuinely rare case where the process holding the lock crashed or was killed and never released it on its own. Running force-unlock while that apply might still legitimately be in progress is exactly the state corruption this entire mechanism exists to prevent -- two writers could now interleave against the same state. So the answer is: check the `Who` and the elapsed time first, confirm with Alice (or confirm her process is actually dead) before even considering force-unlock, and only reach for it once you know the lock is genuinely stuck, not just in use.
questions.professionalAnswer: My gut reaction to 'just force-unlock it' is always to slow down first. That error message is actually pretty generous with information -- it tells you exactly who's holding the lock and when they started, so my first move is just to go check: is Alice's apply actually still running, or did something crash and leave this hanging? Ninety-some percent of the time, it's genuinely in progress and the right answer is just to wait, because the lock releases itself the moment the apply finishes. force-unlock exists for the other case -- a process that died mid-apply and never released cleanly -- and running it while something's still legitimately writing to state is exactly how you'd corrupt it, which is the whole thing locking was built to prevent. So no, I wouldn't just run it on a Slack suggestion. I'd confirm the lock is actually stale first.
commonMistakes: Force-unlocking without first checking the Who and timestamp in the error
Assuming every lock error means a stuck or crashed lock
Not knowing that azurerm locks automatically via blob lease while s3 needs a dynamodb_table with a specific schema to do the same
Treating 'wait' as doing nothing, rather than as the correct, deliberate first response
Forgetting locking only coordinates writes within the same remote backend, not across independent local copies
keyPoints: Locking prevents concurrent writes from corrupting state
The error message names who holds the lock and when it started
Waiting for the current operation to finish is almost always the correct first move
force-unlock is only appropriate for a confirmed-dead process, not a lock that's merely in use
Backend-specific locking mechanisms differ (azurerm blob lease vs. s3 DynamoDB table)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly interprets the lock error and what it protects against
Correctly advises checking Who/timestamp before acting
Correctly scopes force-unlock to confirmed-stuck locks only
Mentions the backend-specific locking mechanism difference
Clarity

questions.title: Workspaces or Separate State Files for a Regulated Environment
questions.prompt: Your company's compliance policy says only the production-support team may even view production infrastructure's Terraform state -- not just apply to it, view it. You currently manage dev, staging, and prod with Terraform workspaces against one shared backend. Does that setup satisfy the policy? Walk through the real tradeoff between workspaces and separate per-environment state files, and design the structure you'd actually move to.
questions.modelAnswer:
No, the current workspace setup does not satisfy this policy. All workspaces in one backend share the same backend, the same provider block, and almost always the same credentials and permissions -- there's no built-in mechanism to grant an identity access to only the prod workspace's state while blocking dev and staging, because they're all just named state files sitting inside the same storage location with the same access boundary. If a credential can reach the backend at all, it can reach every workspace in it, so 'only prod-support can view prod state' is architecturally impossible to enforce with workspaces alone, no matter how carefully the workspaces are named or scoped in CI.

The fix is a directory-per-environment layout: `envs/dev`, `envs/staging`, `envs/prod`, each with its own `backend.tf` pointing at a genuinely different storage account or bucket -- not just a different key within the same one. Each storage location gets its own access policy; prod's storage account gets a narrow role assignment limited to the production-support team, and dev's and staging's don't. All three directories call the same shared modules underneath (the Chapter 4 pattern), so there's no duplication of the actual infrastructure logic -- only the state/backend boundary differs between environments.

The real cost of this move is honest: every environment directory now needs its own backend.tf to maintain, and nothing enforces that each one calls the shared modules correctly the way a single shared config file would -- that consistency becomes a review and process responsibility instead of something the tooling guarantees for you.
questions.professionalAnswer: My honest first answer here is no, workspaces don't cut it for this policy, and I'd want to explain why clearly rather than just assert it. All the workspaces in a setup like this are hitting the same backend with the same credentials -- there's no way to say 'only this identity can see the prod workspace' when prod and dev are really just different state files in the same storage account with the same access policy. If a credential can reach the backend at all, it can reach every workspace in it. So I'd move to separate directories per environment, each pointing at its own backend -- its own storage account or bucket, not just a different key -- so prod's access policy can actually be narrower than dev's. The tradeoff I'd be upfront about is that now you've got more backend.tf files to keep consistent, and nothing automatically enforces that they're all calling the same shared module correctly -- that becomes a review discipline instead of something the tooling guarantees.
commonMistakes: Assuming different workspace names create different permission boundaries
Thinking a different key within the same storage account/bucket is sufficient isolation
Forgetting both approaches can combine -- separate directories for the hard boundary, shared modules underneath for consistency
Overlooking the added maintenance burden of N backend.tf files that nothing keeps in sync automatically
Applying access control only at the service-principal/CI layer and forgetting human read access to the backend storage itself
keyPoints: Workspace isolation gap: all workspaces in one backend share the same credentials and permissions
Real isolation requires a separate backend/storage location per environment, not just separate workspace names
Access policy has to be applied at the storage-account/bucket level, not just within Terraform
Shared modules underneath separate directories keep consistency even with separate state
Combining directories (for the boundary) with modules (for reuse) is the common real-world pattern

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies workspaces don't satisfy the policy, and why
Explains the real isolation gap (shared backend/credentials)
Designs a correct separate-directory structure with distinct backends
Addresses access policy at the storage/backend layer
Notes the combined directories-plus-shared-modules pattern

lessonLink.label: Review: Workspaces vs. Separate State Files: The Real Tradeoff

questions.title: Choosing (and Defending) a Remote Backend's Locking Model
questions.prompt: You're writing the platform's first ADR for how Terraform state will be managed across both Azure and AWS workloads. One reviewer asks why the Azure-hosted projects' backend configuration doesn't mention anything about locking, while the AWS-hosted ones require an extra DynamoDB table resource to be stood up first. Write the explanation you'd put in that ADR, including why the AWS path has to be bootstrapped outside the config it protects.
questions.modelAnswer:
The asymmetry is real and worth documenting explicitly, because it's easy for a reviewer to assume it's an oversight rather than a genuine platform difference.

The `azurerm` backend locks state automatically, using Azure Blob Storage's native lease mechanism -- a built-in feature that lets a client claim temporary exclusive ownership of a blob. There's no extra argument to set and no extra resource to provision; the same `resource_group_name` / `storage_account_name` / `container_name` / `key` block that configures the backend also gets locking for free.

S3 has no equivalent native primitive, so the `s3` backend coordinates locks through a separate DynamoDB table, referenced by the `dynamodb_table` argument. That table has a fixed, required schema: a primary key named `LockID`, of type String -- Terraform writes and deletes a row keyed on the state file's path to claim and release the lock.

The table has to be provisioned ahead of time, in a bootstrap configuration that does not itself use the `s3` backend it's creating supporting infrastructure for. This is a genuine chicken-and-egg problem: a configuration can't store its own state in a backend whose lock table doesn't exist yet. So the lock table gets created once, via local state (or an already-established separate backend), before any 'real' project's s3-backed config ever references `dynamodb_table` -- and the ADR should name this bootstrap step explicitly as a one-time, separately-run piece of infrastructure, not part of the normal per-project Terraform lifecycle.
questions.professionalAnswer: If someone asked me this in a design review, I'd want to normalize that this asymmetry is real and not a mistake in the Azure config. Azure gets locking basically for free -- blob storage has a native lease mechanism, so the same backend block that points at the storage account already protects you from concurrent writes, no extra resource needed. S3 just doesn't have that built in, so the backend leans on a DynamoDB table instead, and that table has to have a very specific shape -- a String primary key literally named LockID. The part I'd flag as the trickiest bit is that you can't create that table in the same state you're going to lock with it -- that's a chicken-and-egg problem, so it has to get bootstrapped once, separately, before the real project ever references it as its dynamodb_table.
commonMistakes: Assuming s3 should get locking for free the way azurerm does, with zero extra setup
Trying to create the dynamodb_table resource inside the same configuration that uses it as its own backend's lock table
Using the wrong primary key name or type on the table (it must be LockID, type String)
Treating remote state alone as sufficient for concurrency safety, without the locking layer
Not documenting the asymmetry, leaving future engineers confused about why one cloud's setup looks different
keyPoints: azurerm backend locks automatically via native blob lease, no extra config
s3 backend requires a separate DynamoDB table via the dynamodb_table argument
The lock table's schema must be a String primary key named LockID
The lock table must be bootstrapped outside the configuration it protects
This is a genuine platform asymmetry worth recording explicitly in an ADR

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains azurerm's automatic lease-based locking
Correctly explains s3's DynamoDB requirement and exact schema
Explains why the table must be bootstrapped separately
Frames the explanation in a way appropriate for an ADR
Clarity

questions.title: Scaling One Module to Thirty Teams Without Losing Control
questions.prompt: Your `network` module (one VNet, standard NSG, naming convention baked in) started in a single project's folder. Eighteen months later, roughly thirty teams across the org want to consume it, and three different teams have already started maintaining their own copy-pasted variants that have quietly drifted apart. Design the real fix: where the module should live, how teams should consume it, and how you'd stop version drift from recurring, referencing the specific mechanisms Terraform actually gives you for this.
questions.modelAnswer:
Move the module out of any single project's folder into its own Git repository, or publish it into a private module registry via Terraform Cloud or Enterprise -- an org-scoped catalog for internal modules, consumed exactly the way the public Terraform Registry is. Publish it under semantic-version git tags (`v1.2.0`, etc.) rather than letting consumers track a moving branch.

Every consuming team's `module` block then pins a version: `version = "~> 1.2"` against a registry source, or `source = "...git...//network?ref=v1.2.0"` for a git source -- remembering the `version` argument only does anything for registry sources, so the `?ref=` is the actual pin for anyone consuming from git directly. Pinning is what actually stops drift going forward: an unreviewed breaking change the module's maintainers push doesn't land in any consuming team's infrastructure until that team deliberately bumps their pin and runs `terraform init -upgrade`.

At thirty-teams scale, the real value of the registry over 'just a shared git repo' isn't the publishing mechanism itself -- it's that there's now one reviewed, versioned source of truth every team consumes identically, instead of three (and eventually more) teams' copy-pasted variants that nobody is auditing against each other. The three existing forks get migrated deliberately: replace their inline resource blocks with a module call pinned at whatever version matches their current behavior first, verify `plan` shows no unexpected changes, then upgrade from there on a normal change-review cadence -- never a silent, forced cutover.
questions.professionalAnswer: At thirty teams, I wouldn't keep the module sitting in one project's folder -- that's basically asking for the exact copy-paste drift that's already started with those three forks. I'd move it into its own repo, tagged with real semantic versions, and ideally published into a private registry if we're on Terraform Cloud, since that's literally what that feature is for. The part that actually stops the drift going forward is pinning -- version for a registry source, a ref on the URL if it's sourced from git directly, and people sometimes think version works for both, but it does nothing on a git source. I'd also be upfront that just having a registry doesn't fix the three existing forks by itself -- I'd want a real migration plan to bring those onto the shared module at whatever version matches their current behavior, then upgrade them deliberately from there.
commonMistakes: Leaving the module inside one team's project folder and telling others to 'just copy it', recreating the same drift problem at larger scale
Publishing without semantic version tags, so every consumer tracks a moving target
Using the version argument on a git source and assuming it pins anything
Having no migration plan for the three already-forked copies, leaving fragmentation to continue alongside the new shared module
Treating 'we have a registry now' as solving governance by itself, without a review process around publishing new versions
keyPoints: Move the module to its own versioned repository or private registry
Private module registry is Terraform Cloud/Enterprise's org-scoped catalog, consumed like the public one
Pinning (version for registry sources, ?ref= for git sources) is what actually prevents drift going forward
Migrate the existing forked copies deliberately rather than leaving them to diverge further
Governance/review process around publishing new versions matters as much as the mechanism itself

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly proposes moving the module to its own versioned repo/registry
Correctly distinguishes version vs. ?ref= pinning mechanisms
Explains why pinning is what actually stops drift going forward
Addresses migrating the existing forked copies deliberately
Addresses governance/review of new module versions

questions.title: Moving a Team Off Local State Without a Big-Bang Cutover
questions.prompt: You join a team that's been running Terraform for a year, with `terraform.tfstate` committed straight into the project's git repo and everyone running `apply` from their own laptop whenever they feel like it. Tell me about how you'd actually go about fixing this -- not just what the right end state looks like, but how you'd introduce the change to a team that doesn't think there's a problem yet, since nothing has visibly broken for them so far.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd treat this as a low-drama migration to lead, not a mandate to issue. First, I'd make the risk concrete rather than abstract: pull up the currently-committed `terraform.tfstate` and show the team what's actually sitting in their git history in plain text -- a database password or storage key almost certainly got captured by some past resource, and that's now permanent, readable by anyone with repo access, even after rotation. That's a far more persuasive argument than citing 'best practice.' Second, I'd name the independent risk they haven't been burned by yet: two people applying within the same window with no locking can silently corrupt state or overwrite each other's work -- not having hit this yet is luck, not safety.

Then I'd propose the fix as a single, low-risk, one-time migration rather than something everyone does independently: stand up a remote backend with locking (blob lease for Azure, a DynamoDB table with a LockID/String key for S3, with bucket versioning on), add the backend block, run `terraform init`, and answer 'yes' to the 'copy existing state to the new backend' prompt -- nothing about the real infrastructure changes, only where the state record lives. Immediately after, I'd add `*.tfstate` to `.gitignore` and remove the tracked file going forward, while flagging separately that the secrets already in git history still need a rotation conversation, since the migration itself doesn't erase history. I'd schedule this as one coordinated window with a single person driving the actual migration command, not N people migrating their own checkouts independently -- which would recreate exactly the coordination problem the migration exists to fix.
questions.professionalAnswer: Honestly, the first thing I'd do is not lecture anyone -- I'd just open the committed tfstate file in front of them and let them see what's actually in it. Nine times out of ten there's a connection string or an access key sitting right there in plaintext, and that lands a lot harder than me saying 'this isn't best practice.' Then I'd point out the second problem separately, because it's easy to miss: right now, if two of us ran apply in the same five minutes, nothing stops that from corrupting the state file, and the only reason it hasn't happened is luck, not design. From there I'd keep the actual fix boring and low-risk -- stand up a real backend with locking, run init, say yes when it asks to copy the state over, done. I'd make a point of doing that migration myself, once, in a scheduled window, rather than asking everyone to migrate their own checkout, because that second approach just recreates the same multiple-people-touching-state problem we're trying to get rid of. And I'd flag, separately and honestly, that whatever secrets are already sitting in git history from the old committed state file still need to get rotated -- the migration doesn't make that history disappear.
commonMistakes: Leading with 'this is against best practice' instead of a concrete, team-specific risk
Trying to migrate everyone's local checkout independently instead of one coordinated cutover
Forgetting to raise the secret-rotation conversation for what's already exposed in git history
Adding remote state without also adding locking, fixing only half the problem
Treating this as a one-off config change rather than explaining it so the team understands why it matters going forward
keyPoints: Lead with a concrete, team-specific risk (exposed secrets, no coordination) rather than abstract best-practice
Propose remote backend plus locking as one combined fix, not two separate efforts
Use the real terraform init migration prompt rather than manually copying state
Coordinate as one driven cutover, not N independent migrations
Address the already-exposed secrets separately as a rotation follow-up

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Demonstrates ownership with a concrete, low-drama change plan rather than a mandate
Correctly identifies both real risks (exposed secrets, no locking)
Correctly describes the actual migration mechanism (backend block, init, copy-state prompt)
Addresses communication and coordination with the team
Addresses the secret-rotation follow-up

questions.title: Pushing Back on an Unattended Production Apply
questions.prompt: A teammate who's excited about 'moving fast' sets up a pipeline that runs `terraform apply -auto-approve` on every merge to main, for a production AWS environment, with no approval step. They ask for your sign-off in the PR review. Walk me through how you'd actually handle that conversation -- what you'd say, and what you'd propose instead.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd start by naming what's already right about it -- plan running automatically on every PR is good, and I wouldn't want to undo that. Then I'd name precisely why apply is a different risk class than a typical app deployment: a bad application deploy is usually recoverable in seconds by rolling back to the previous image, but a bad `terraform apply` can delete a production database, replace infrastructure other resources depend on, or lock out real traffic -- and some of that isn't simply reversible by redeploying something. That asymmetry, not a blanket fear of automation, is the actual reason to gate it.

I'd propose the concrete, low-friction fix rather than just blocking the PR: keep the trigger exactly as automatic as it is (push to main still fires immediately), and add one line -- `environment: production` -- tying the apply job to a GitHub Environment with required reviewers configured, so the job pauses and waits for a named approver instead of running unattended. Everything else about the pipeline, including the automatic plan-on-PR, stays exactly as fast as it already was. If the team were on Terraform Cloud instead, the equivalent is switching that workspace to Manual Apply, so runs pause after plan for a human to confirm.

I'd frame the ask as 'let's keep this exactly as automated as it is today, just add the one gate that matches the actual blast radius of this specific job' rather than relitigating the whole pipeline or implying the teammate did something careless.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't come in hot on this one, because the instinct to automate isn't wrong -- the plan-on-every-PR part is genuinely good, and I'd say so first. But I'd be direct about the one gap: applying to prod automatically on every merge treats a Terraform apply like a container rollout, and it just isn't one. If this goes wrong, I can't just redeploy the previous build to fix it -- it might have deleted something, or reconfigured a security group in a way that's actively locking out traffic right now. So my ask wouldn't be 'turn off automation,' it'd be 'let's add exactly one line.' GitHub Environments let you require a named reviewer before a job runs, so the trigger stays automatic and the only thing that changes is there's a human in the loop right before the destructive step specifically. If they were using Terraform Cloud instead I'd point them at Manual Apply, which does the same thing at the platform level. I'd rather land that as a quick addition to their existing PR than as a blocker that makes it feel like I'm vetoing the whole idea.
commonMistakes: Treating automation itself as the problem rather than the specific missing human gate
Blocking the PR outright instead of proposing the specific one-line fix
Not acknowledging what the teammate got right (automatic plan-on-PR)
Forgetting the Terraform Cloud equivalent for teams not using GitHub Actions
Framing the pushback as a rule rather than explaining the actual asymmetry that justifies it
keyPoints: Name the real asymmetry (reversible app deploy vs. destructive infra change) as the reason, not a blanket rule
Propose environment: production plus required reviewers as the concrete fix
Keep the rest of the pipeline exactly as automated as it already was
Know the Terraform Cloud equivalent (Manual Apply)
Handle the conversation collaboratively, acknowledging what's already good

evaluationCriteria.criterion: States the real reasoning (asymmetric risk) rather than generic caution
Proposes the correct concrete technical fix (environment/required reviewers)
Preserves the good parts of the existing pipeline rather than over-correcting
Mentions the Terraform Cloud equivalent
Collaborative, non-confrontational framing

questions.title: Why Editing a Deployment Creates a Brand-New ReplicaSet
questions.prompt: A teammate asks why Kubernetes doesn't just edit the existing ReplicaSet's Pods in place when they change a Deployment's container image -- wouldn't that be simpler than creating an entirely new ReplicaSet? Explain the real parent/child relationship between Deployments, ReplicaSets, and Pods, exactly what each layer's reconciliation loop checks, and why that architecture makes the 'new ReplicaSet' behavior the only way a rolling update and a rollback can both work.
questions.modelAnswer:
A ReplicaSet's reconciliation loop checks exactly one thing: how many Pods matching its template currently exist, versus how many should. It never edits a running Pod's spec -- it only ever creates or deletes whole Pods to correct the count, which means a ReplicaSet has no mechanism at all for changing what's already running. If you edited a ReplicaSet's template directly, existing Pods would keep running their old image forever, because reconciling count is the only thing that loop does.

A Deployment sits one layer above and manages the thing a ReplicaSet can't: controlled change over time. When a Deployment's Pod template changes -- a new image tag, new env vars, anything -- the Deployment controller creates a brand-new ReplicaSet carrying that new template, scales it up gradually while scaling the old ReplicaSet down, and only deletes the old ReplicaSet (by scaling it to zero, not removing it outright) once the new one is fully healthy. That's the entire mechanism of a rolling update, and it's also exactly why a rollback is possible without reapplying an old YAML file: the previous ReplicaSet wasn't deleted, just scaled to zero, so undoing a Deployment is simply scaling that old ReplicaSet back up and the current one back down -- the same mechanism as a forward rollout, run in reverse.

So the layered design isn't incidental complexity: a ReplicaSet's narrow job (count only, never content) is precisely what makes it safe for a Deployment to swap ReplicaSets wholesale instead of mutating one in place, and that wholesale swap, plus keeping old ReplicaSets around at zero replicas, is what gives you both a gradual rollout and an instant rollback for free.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it by walking up the chain. A ReplicaSet genuinely only does one job -- make sure the Pod count matches the template, nothing about changing what's already running. So if Kubernetes tried to 'just edit the Pods in place,' there's actually no mechanism in a ReplicaSet for that at all; it would need entirely new logic bolted on. Instead, a Deployment handles change by creating a whole new ReplicaSet with the new template and shifting replicas from old to new gradually -- which is the rolling update everyone's familiar with. The part people don't always connect is that this is also exactly why rollback works instantly: Kubernetes doesn't delete the old ReplicaSet when it's done, it just scales it down to zero and leaves it sitting there as a revision record. Rolling back is just scaling that old one back up and the new one back down -- same mechanism, opposite direction. It's a clean design specifically because each layer does one narrow thing.
commonMistakes: Thinking a ReplicaSet can reconcile 'content' (the Pod template) the same way it reconciles count
Believing a Deployment edits existing Pods in place rather than creating a new ReplicaSet
Not realizing old ReplicaSets are scaled to zero, not deleted, which is what makes rollback possible
Assuming rollback requires reapplying an old manifest file rather than being a built-in Deployment operation
Confusing a Deployment's rollout strategy settings (maxSurge/maxUnavailable) with the ReplicaSet-swap mechanism itself
keyPoints: A ReplicaSet's reconciliation loop checks count only, never content
A Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet for any Pod template change
The Deployment scales the new ReplicaSet up and the old one down gradually
Old ReplicaSets are scaled to zero, not deleted, serving as revision history
Rollback is the same create-new-ReplicaSet mechanism run in reverse, requiring no YAML reapply

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains a ReplicaSet reconciles count only, never content
Correctly explains a Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet per template change
Explains old ReplicaSets are scaled to zero, not deleted
Connects this mechanism to why rollback works without reapplying YAML
Clarity

questions.title: Why LoadBalancer Is a Superset, and What It Costs at Scale
questions.prompt: Explain, precisely, why Kubernetes documentation and most architects describe `NodePort` as a strict superset of `ClusterIP`, and `LoadBalancer` as a strict superset of `NodePort`. Then explain the real, specific problem that creates for a cluster running thirty HTTP services behind thirty `LoadBalancer` Services, and why Ingress is the thing that actually solves it.
questions.modelAnswer:
Each Service type literally includes everything the type below it does, plus one additional capability. `ClusterIP` gives a stable virtual IP and DNS name reachable only from inside the cluster, with kube-proxy load-balancing traffic to healthy Pod endpoints behind it. `NodePort` does everything `ClusterIP` does -- the virtual IP, the endpoint tracking, all of it still exists -- and additionally opens the same fixed port (30000-32767 by default) on every node, forwarding external traffic that arrives there into the Service. `LoadBalancer` does everything `NodePort` does -- including that same opened node port underneath -- and additionally asks the cloud provider's controller to provision a real external load balancer that targets that NodePort across every node. Each layer is strictly additive, never a replacement of the layer below.

The specific problem at thirty services: each `LoadBalancer` Service typically provisions its own dedicated cloud load balancer -- its own Azure Load Balancer or AWS ELB/NLB, each with its own cost, its own public IP, and its own provisioning lifecycle. Thirty HTTP services means thirty separate cloud load balancers, paid for and managed independently, just to route HTTP(S) traffic that could reasonably share one entry point based on hostname or path.

Ingress solves this by sitting in front of many Services behind a single shared load balancer (fronting an Ingress controller, which is itself usually exposed via one `LoadBalancer` Service). The Ingress resource's host/path rules then route incoming HTTP(S) traffic to the correct backend Service internally, so thirty HTTP services can share one external load balancer and one public IP instead of thirty of each -- a real cost and operational-complexity win that only applies to HTTP(S) traffic specifically, which is why a non-HTTP protocol or a service that genuinely needs its own dedicated external endpoint still reaches for `LoadBalancer` directly.
questions.professionalAnswer: The way I'd explain this to someone is that each Service type is really just the one before it plus one more thing bolted on -- ClusterIP gives you the internal virtual IP, NodePort keeps all of that and just opens a fixed port on every node too, and LoadBalancer keeps the NodePort underneath and asks the cloud to provision a real external load balancer in front of it. The cost problem only shows up once you're running a lot of these -- each LoadBalancer Service usually means its own separate cloud load balancer, so thirty HTTP services means thirty of those, each with its own bill and its own public IP. That's exactly the gap Ingress fills -- it sits in front of all of them behind one shared load balancer and routes by hostname or path internally, so you're paying for one entry point instead of thirty. I'd also flag that this only really helps for HTTP traffic specifically -- something needing raw TCP or its own dedicated IP still reaches for LoadBalancer directly.
commonMistakes: Describing the three Service types as unrelated alternatives rather than a strict superset chain
Not knowing LoadBalancer still opens the underlying NodePort even though you don't interact with it directly
Assuming Ingress replaces Services entirely, rather than routing to them
Missing that the cost problem is specifically about one cloud load balancer per LoadBalancer Service
Recommending Ingress for a workload that genuinely needs raw TCP or its own dedicated external IP, where Ingress doesn't fit
keyPoints: ClusterIP: internal virtual IP; NodePort adds a fixed port on every node; LoadBalancer adds a provisioned cloud LB
Each type is strictly additive over the one before it, never a replacement
Each LoadBalancer Service typically provisions its own separate cloud load balancer
At scale, many LoadBalancer Services means many redundant, separately-billed load balancers
Ingress fronts many Services behind one shared load balancer, routing HTTP(S) by host/path

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the superset relationship between the three Service types
Correctly identifies the per-Service cloud load balancer cost problem at scale
Correctly explains how Ingress solves it (shared LB, host/path routing)
Notes the HTTP(S)-specific scope of Ingress's solution

questions.title: Writing a Multi-Stage Dockerfile That Ships Only the Binary
questions.prompt: You're containerizing a Go service. A single-stage Dockerfile built on `golang:1.23` works correctly but ships the entire Go toolchain in the final image. Write a corrected, multi-stage Dockerfile that produces a minimal final image, and explain exactly what `COPY --from=<stage>` does and doesn't carry forward from the earlier stage.
questions.modelAnswer:
The fix separates the build phase, which needs the full compiler toolchain, from the runtime phase, which only needs the compiled binary:

```dockerfile
# Stage 1: build, using the full toolchain
FROM golang:1.23 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o server .

# Stage 2: runtime, starting completely fresh
FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12
COPY --from=build /app/server /server
ENTRYPOINT ["/server"]
```

`FROM golang:1.23 AS build` names the first stage; the second `FROM` starts an entirely new, unrelated base image, and none of the first stage's layers carry over automatically just by existing in the same file. `COPY --from=build /app/server /server` is the one instruction doing the real work: it reaches back into the `build` stage's filesystem and copies out exactly the one file named -- the compiled binary -- into the new, otherwise-empty runtime image.

What it does carry forward: only the specific file(s) or directory named in the `COPY --from` instruction, exactly as they exist in that stage at that point. What it does not carry forward: everything else in the `build` stage -- the Go compiler, the module cache, the source files, the Debian userland underneath `golang:1.23` -- none of that exists in the final image at all, because the final image was never built from the `build` stage's layers in the first place; it started from `gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12` and only ever received the one file explicitly copied in.
questions.professionalAnswer: The way I'd frame it: this Dockerfile has two completely separate 'FROM's, and that's the whole trick. The first stage, named build, uses the full golang:1.23 image because it genuinely needs the compiler to produce the binary. The second stage throws all of that away and starts from a tiny distroless base that has basically nothing in it -- no shell, no package manager. The only bridge between them is that one COPY --from=build line, which reaches into the first stage and pulls out exactly the compiled server binary, nothing else. Everything else that was sitting in the build stage -- the compiler, the module cache, all of it -- just never makes it into the final image, because the final image was never built on top of that stage's layers to begin with. People sometimes assume naming a stage somehow links its layers into the final image; it doesn't. Only what you explicitly COPY --from makes the trip.
commonMistakes: Assuming the build stage's layers automatically carry into the final image just by being in the same Dockerfile
Forgetting to set CGO_ENABLED=0 for a static binary when targeting a distroless/scratch base with no C library
Copying the wrong path from the build stage, breaking the final COPY --from
Not realizing docker build runs every stage by default unless --target is used
Choosing a runtime base that still needs a shell/package manager when a true distroless image would work and be smaller
keyPoints: Multi-stage builds use multiple FROM instructions, each an independent stage
AS <name> labels a stage for later reference
COPY --from=<stage> copies only the named files, not any other layer from that stage
The final image is built from whatever the last FROM starts, not accumulated from earlier stages
Distroless/minimal runtime bases are only possible once the build toolchain is fully decoupled

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct multi-stage Dockerfile with named build stage
Correct COPY --from usage targeting the right artifact
Explains what COPY --from does carry forward
Explains what it does not carry forward and why
Clarity

questions.title: A Least-Privilege RBAC Setup for a Billing Reporting Job
questions.prompt: A Pod running a nightly billing report needs to read (not modify) Pods and their logs, inside the `payments` namespace only. Write the real Kubernetes objects needed to give it exactly that access using a dedicated identity -- not the namespace's `default` ServiceAccount -- and show the command you'd run to verify the access is correctly scoped, both for what it should be able to do and what it should be refused.
questions.modelAnswer:
This needs three objects: a dedicated ServiceAccount (so this workload's identity is distinguishable from every other Pod sharing the default identity), a namespaced Role granting only the read verbs on exactly the resources needed, and a RoleBinding tying that Role to that ServiceAccount inside the same namespace.

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: billing-reader
  namespace: payments
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: pod-reader
  namespace: payments
rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["pods", "pods/log"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: read-pods
  namespace: payments
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: billing-reader
    namespace: payments
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: pod-reader
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
```

A `Role` (not a `ClusterRole`) keeps this scoped to the `payments` namespace only, with no reach anywhere else even if someone later binds it incorrectly. `get`/`list`/`watch` are the read-only verbs; nothing here grants `create`, `update`, `patch`, or `delete`. A `RoleBinding` (not a `ClusterRoleBinding`) keeps the grant itself namespace-scoped too.

To verify, ask the API server directly rather than assuming:

```
kubectl auth can-i get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:payments:billing-reader -n payments
yes

kubectl auth can-i delete pods --as=system:serviceaccount:payments:billing-reader -n payments
no
```

The Pod itself then references this identity with `serviceAccountName: billing-reader` in its spec, instead of silently running as the namespace's `default` ServiceAccount.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd build this the way I'd build any least-privilege access -- start with a dedicated identity, not the namespace's default ServiceAccount, because sharing 'default' across every workload makes it impossible to reason about who can do what later. Then a namespaced Role, not a ClusterRole, with just get/list/watch on pods and pods/log -- nothing that writes, and nothing that reaches outside the payments namespace. I'd bind that with a RoleBinding, again scoped to the namespace, not a ClusterRoleBinding. And I wouldn't just assume it's right -- I'd actually run kubectl auth can-i against the service account for both something it should be able to do and something it shouldn't, because that's the only way to confirm the scoping actually landed the way I intended instead of just trusting the YAML looks right.
questions.example:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: billing-report
  namespace: payments
spec:
  serviceAccountName: billing-reader
  containers:
    - name: report
      image: billing-report:1.0
commonMistakes: Letting the Pod run as the namespace's default ServiceAccount instead of a dedicated one
Using a ClusterRole/ClusterRoleBinding when a namespaced Role/RoleBinding is all that's needed
Granting broader verbs (e.g. list on all resources, or write verbs) than the job actually needs
Forgetting pods/log is a separate resource from pods and must be listed explicitly to read logs
Assuming the permission is correct without actually running kubectl auth can-i to verify both allowed and denied cases
keyPoints: Dedicated ServiceAccount per workload, not the shared default
Namespaced Role with only the exact apiGroups/resources/verbs needed
RoleBinding (not ClusterRoleBinding) to keep the grant namespace-scoped
pods and pods/log are separate resources that must both be listed for log access
kubectl auth can-i verifies both the allowed and the correctly-denied cases

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct dedicated ServiceAccount, not default
Correct least-privilege Role (right resources/verbs only)
Correct RoleBinding scoping the grant to the namespace
Correct kubectl auth can-i verification for both allow and deny
Clarity

questions.title: Diagnosing a Node Where Everything Started Dying
questions.prompt: `kubectl get pods -o wide` shows this on one node: `order-worker` as `OOMKilled`, `nightly-report` as `Error`, and `order-api` as `Evicted` -- all at once, all on `node-3`. Nobody changed `order-worker` or `order-api`'s manifests recently. Walk through how you'd find the real root cause, explain the difference between a pod being OOMKilled and a pod being Evicted (both appear here), and give the fix at both the single-manifest level and the platform level so this specific failure mode can't recur.
questions.modelAnswer:
The fact that three unrelated pods failed together on the same node, with two of them unchanged, is the real clue -- this isn't three separate bugs, it's one pod destabilizing its neighbors. The investigation starts with `kubectl describe pod nightly-report-...` and the CronJob's manifest: if it has no `resources.requests`/`resources.limits` block at all, it gets Kubernetes' `BestEffort` QoS class, the lowest priority, and critically no memory ceiling -- it keeps allocating memory as long as the node has any free, because nothing is telling the kernel to stop it earlier. If an upstream schema change made that night's query return an unusually large result set, its memory use would climb without bound.

OOMKilled and Evicted are two different mechanisms, both real, both triggered by the same underlying memory pressure. `order-worker` showing OOMKilled means the Linux kernel's OOMKiller itself picked that specific process and sent it SIGKILL because it scored as the best candidate once the node ran genuinely out of memory -- that scoring is the kernel's own heuristic, not necessarily 'the pod that caused the problem.' `order-api` showing Evicted means the kubelet proactively removed that pod from the node to relieve system-wide memory pressure, before the kernel had to intervene at all. Neither `order-worker` nor `order-api` did anything wrong; both were healthy, correctly-configured pods caught in the blast radius of a neighbor with no ceiling on its own memory use.

The immediate fix is adding a real `resources` block to the CronJob's container, with both `requests` (what the scheduler uses to decide whether a node has room, preventing this pod from being packed too tightly in the first place) and `limits` (a true ceiling, so a runaway query gets that one container OOMKilled on its own and retried by the CronJob, instead of destabilizing the whole node). The platform-level fix is adding a `LimitRange` to every namespace, supplying default `requests`/`limits` automatically to any container admitted without its own -- so the next engineer who copies an old manifest and forgets a resources block gets safe defaults automatically instead of a repeat of this exact incident.
questions.professionalAnswer: What jumps out at me immediately is that three unrelated pods failed on the same node at the same time, and two of them hadn't been touched recently -- that's not three bugs, that's one pod taking its neighbors down with it. I'd go straight to the CronJob and check if it has a resources block at all, because no limits means BestEffort QoS and literally no ceiling on memory -- it just keeps eating whatever's free. From there I'd explain the two different things that happened on that node: OOMKilled means the kernel's own OOMKiller picked a process and killed it because it looked like the best candidate once memory ran out, and Evicted means the kubelet proactively pulled a pod off the node before it got that bad. Neither of the other two pods did anything wrong. The actual fix is adding real requests and limits to that CronJob so a runaway query only takes down its own container -- but the fix that actually matters platform-wide is a LimitRange, so the next engineer who copies an old manifest and forgets a resources block gets safe defaults instead of a repeat of this.
questions.example:
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: "100m"
    memory: "128Mi"
  limits:
    cpu: "500m"
    memory: "512Mi"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: default-resource-limits
spec:
  limits:
    - type: Container
      default: { cpu: "500m", memory: "512Mi" }
      defaultRequest: { cpu: "100m", memory: "128Mi" }
commonMistakes: Investigating order-worker and order-api's own manifests first, since they're the ones that visibly failed
Treating OOMKilled and Evicted as the same failure mode rather than two distinct mechanisms
Fixing only the one CronJob manifest without adding a namespace-wide LimitRange
Forgetting that requests (not just limits) matter for scheduler packing, not only runaway memory
Assuming BestEffort QoS just means 'lower priority' without connecting it to 'no memory ceiling at all'
keyPoints: A pod with no requests/limits gets BestEffort QoS and no memory ceiling
One unlimited pod's memory growth can destabilize every pod sharing its node
OOMKilled: the kernel's OOMKiller kills a scored-candidate process
Evicted: the kubelet proactively removes a pod to relieve node-wide pressure
Fix at two levels: add requests/limits to the specific manifest, and a namespace-wide LimitRange as the platform-level guardrail

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the real root cause (unlimited neighbor pod) rather than the visibly failing pods
Correctly distinguishes OOMKilled vs. Evicted
Gives the correct manifest-level fix (requests and limits)
Gives the correct platform-level fix (LimitRange)
Clarity

questions.title: A NetworkPolicy That Doesn't Seem to Do Anything
questions.prompt: A teammate deploys a `default-deny-all` NetworkPolicy plus a narrow allow-rule for `frontend` to reach `payments-api`, expecting all other traffic in the `billing` namespace to now be blocked. After applying it, every pod can still reach every other pod exactly as before. Walk through the two completely different root causes this could be, how you'd check for each one, and why 'the YAML looks correct' doesn't rule either of them out.
questions.modelAnswer:
Root cause one: the cluster's CNI plugin doesn't enforce NetworkPolicy at all. The `NetworkPolicy` resource is just a declarative rule set -- it only takes effect if the installed CNI plugin (Calico, Cilium, Azure CNI with policy support, etc.) actually reads and enforces it. Some CNI setups, notably basic kubenet-style configurations, simply ignore NetworkPolicy objects entirely; they apply successfully (`kubectl apply` succeeds, `kubectl get networkpolicy` shows them existing), but nothing in the data path is actually restricting traffic. The check here is confirming which CNI plugin the cluster runs and whether its documentation lists NetworkPolicy enforcement as supported -- not re-reading the YAML.

Root cause two, assuming the CNI does enforce policy: a label mismatch between the policy's selectors and the actual pods. `podSelector: {}` in the deny-all policy selects pods by label match in the `billing` namespace -- if that policy was accidentally scoped with a non-empty `podSelector` that doesn't actually match the intended pods, or if it was applied to the wrong namespace, it silently protects nothing. Similarly, the allow-rule's `from.podSelector` matching `app: frontend` only works if the frontend pods are actually labeled exactly that way -- a label typo, or pods created before a labeling convention changed, would leave the allow-rule matching zero real pods without any error being raised.

'The YAML looks correct' doesn't rule out either cause because both failure modes are invisible from reading the manifest alone: a non-enforcing CNI makes a perfectly correct policy a no-op, and a label mismatch is a runtime fact about the actual running pods, not something visible in the policy file itself. The real check is `kubectl describe networkpolicy default-deny-all -n billing` and `kubectl describe networkpolicy allow-frontend-to-api -n billing`, cross-referenced against `kubectl get pods -n billing --show-labels` -- confirming the selectors actually match real pods -- combined with verifying the CNI plugin's NetworkPolicy support directly, since no `kubectl` command can prove enforcement is actually happening if the CNI is silently ignoring the resource.
questions.professionalAnswer: When something like this comes up, I try not to assume the YAML is the problem just because it reads correctly. There are really two separate things that could be going on here, and they don't show up the same way. One is that the cluster's CNI just doesn't enforce NetworkPolicy at all -- some of the more basic setups will let you apply the policy fine and just silently ignore it, so I'd check what CNI we're actually running before anything else. The other is a label mismatch -- maybe the deny-all's podSelector isn't actually matching what it should, or the frontend pods aren't labeled exactly app: frontend the way the allow-rule expects. Neither of those shows up by reading the manifest -- you have to describe the actual policy and cross-reference it against real pod labels with --show-labels to catch the second one, and check the CNI docs or behavior directly to catch the first.
commonMistakes: Assuming NetworkPolicy always takes effect just because it applied without error
Only checking the YAML's syntax rather than cross-referencing selectors against real pod labels
Not knowing some CNI plugins silently ignore NetworkPolicy entirely
Checking only the allow-rule's labels and not the deny-all policy's own podSelector/namespace scope
Treating 'kubectl apply succeeded' as proof the policy is being enforced
keyPoints: NetworkPolicy only works if the cluster's CNI plugin actually enforces it
Some CNI plugins (e.g. basic kubenet setups) silently ignore NetworkPolicy
A label mismatch between a policy's selector and real pod labels is a second, independent root cause
Neither failure mode is visible from the YAML alone; both require runtime verification
kubectl describe networkpolicy plus kubectl get pods --show-labels is the real diagnostic pairing

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies CNI non-enforcement as a root cause
Correctly identifies label/selector mismatch as a separate root cause
Gives correct diagnostic steps for each cause
Explains why valid-looking YAML doesn't rule out either cause
