questions.title: Why No Architecture Optimizes Every Pillar at Once
questions.prompt: A teammate proposes adding active-active failover across two regions for an order-processing API, presenting it as a pure win with no downside. Using the Well-Architected Framework's pillar-tradeoff logic, explain specifically why that framing is wrong, what the fix actually costs and in which other pillar, and the repeatable question you'd use to decide whether the business should pay that cost for this particular workload.
questions.modelAnswer:
No real architecture optimizes every pillar at once, because every design decision spends a shared, finite budget of money, operational complexity, and acceptable risk, and the five pillars are competing claims on that same budget. Presenting active-active failover as a pure win skips naming what it actually costs: direct cost roughly doubles, because you're now running two production-capable clusters instead of one; operational complexity increases, because there are now two regions' worth of deployments, alerts, and a failover runbook that has to actually be tested (an untested failover path is not meaningfully different from having none); and critically, this moves directly against the cost-optimization pillar -- you cannot maximize reliability and minimize cost in the same design.

The repeatable question isn't 'which pillar is objectively right' -- there's no universal formula -- it's: what does this specific workload actually need, measured against what failure in each pillar actually costs this specific business? A payments API with regulatory uptime requirements may genuinely justify the active-active cost; an internal reporting dashboard used twice a month almost certainly doesn't, and its cost-optimization claim on the budget should win over its reliability claim. That's a legitimate, documented architectural decision, not a shortcut -- the pillar that 'wins' for a given workload is a business decision made visible through architecture, never a default.

So the actual fix to the teammate's framing isn't to reject active-active -- it's to name the tradeoff out loud in the proposal itself: 'Adding active-active failover closes the reliability gap, at roughly double the steady-state compute cost and an ongoing commitment to test failover quarterly. Given this workload's actual revenue-per-minute of downtime, is that trade worth making?' That question, asked explicitly, is what a design review is actually for.
questions.professionalAnswer: If a teammate pitched active-active to me as a pure win, the first thing I'd do is just name what it actually costs, because presenting it as free is the real problem, not the idea itself. You're roughly doubling compute spend, because now two regions are both running production-capable capacity, plus you've taken on an ongoing commitment to actually test the failover runbook -- an untested one isn't meaningfully different from having none. And that directly fights the cost pillar; there's no version of this where you get better reliability and lower cost at the same time. The question I'd actually want answered isn't 'is this a good idea in general,' it's 'what does this specific workload's downside look like in dollars, and is that worth what we're about to spend to avoid it.' A payments API might justify it easily. A twice-a-month internal dashboard almost certainly doesn't, and that's not a cop-out -- it's a real, documented call about where the business wants its budget to go.
commonMistakes: Accepting a reliability fix as a 'pure win' without naming what it costs elsewhere
Treating pillar tradeoffs as a flaw in the framework rather than the framework's central lesson
Assuming there's a universal 'right' pillar to prioritize, independent of the specific workload
Not connecting the cost side of the tradeoff to a concrete, specific number (e.g. roughly doubled compute spend)
Treating the decision as purely technical rather than a business decision made visible through architecture
keyPoints: The five pillars compete for the same finite budget of cost, complexity, and risk
Active-active failover's real cost: roughly doubled compute spend plus ongoing operational complexity
This moves directly against the cost-optimization pillar; you cannot maximize both at once
The deciding question is workload-specific: what does failure in each pillar cost this specific business
A sound tradeoff is one named explicitly in the proposal/review, not hidden by framing a fix as free

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why pillars compete for a shared budget
Correctly identifies the specific cost of active-active failover and which pillar it opposes
Gives the correct repeatable, workload-specific deciding question
Clarity

questions.title: Writing an ADR That Actually Records the Tradeoff
questions.prompt: Your team just decided to use AWS Transit Gateway instead of hand-built VPC peering for a platform expanding from 8 to roughly 40 application VPCs across two regions. Write the real ADR for this decision using the four-part format, including at least two genuinely rejected alternatives and a Consequences section that states a real downside, not just the win.
questions.modelAnswer: An ADR is deliberately small -- a record of one decision at one point in time, not a full design document -- and needs exactly four sections: Context (what made the status quo untenable), Options Considered (the real alternatives, including rejected ones), Decision (unambiguous, no hedging), and Consequences (both the upside and the downside accepted to get it). Skipping the rejected alternatives is the most common way an ADR fails, because without them a reader six months later can't tell whether a changed circumstance should reopen the question. Skipping the downside in Consequences turns the record into marketing copy for a decision that was never actually weighed against anything.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd keep this ADR small on purpose -- one decision, not a design doc. Context first: we're going from 8 to 40 VPCs and full mesh peering was already getting painful to review by hand. Then I'd genuinely list what we considered and rejected, not just the winner -- sticking with hand-built peering and a hub NVA was one option, and I'd say plainly why it didn't make the cut, mainly that it's still manual UDR maintenance per VPC. Full mesh at this scale is the other obvious reject, for the connection-count-blowing-up reason. Then the decision itself, stated flat: we're going with Transit Gateway. And the part I'd make sure doesn't get skipped is Consequences -- not just 'it's easier to add a VPC now,' but the real cost too, like the per-GB data processing charge through the TGW that full mesh wouldn't have had, and that we haven't load-tested cross-region TGW peering yet. If the Consequences section only has upsides, it's not really a record of a tradeoff.
questions.example:
# ADR-0021: AWS Transit Gateway for Multi-VPC Connectivity

Status: Accepted
Date: 2026-10-29

## Context
The platform is expanding from 8 to roughly 40 application VPCs across two AWS regions. Our
current approach -- direct VPC peering between any two VPCs that need to reach each other --
already requires manual review of each new peering relationship and its route tables. At 40
VPCs, full-mesh peering would require up to 780 individual peering connections, each needing its
own route and firewall review, which is not operationally sustainable for the platform team to
maintain by hand.

## Options Considered
1. **Continue hand-built VPC peering, hub-and-spoke via a central NVA** -- requires a user-defined
   route per spoke VPC pointing at a hub network virtual appliance. Rejected: AWS VPC peering is
   non-transitive, so this still means manually maintaining a route table entry per spoke, and an
   NVA introduces a throughput bottleneck and an extra component the platform team has to patch
   and scale itself.
2. **Full mesh peering, accepting the manual overhead** -- rejected outright: connection count
   grows quadratically, and there is no natural chokepoint for centralized firewall or logging
   enforcement, which the compliance team requires for cross-VPC traffic.
3. **AWS Transit Gateway** -- a single managed, natively transitive router that VPCs, VPNs, and
   Direct Connect links attach to, with routing behavior controlled via Transit Gateway route
   table associations rather than hand-maintained UDRs per VPC.

## Decision
We will adopt AWS Transit Gateway as the central connectivity hub for all current and future
application VPCs, with a dedicated inspection VPC attached to the TGW route table that all
cross-VPC and egress traffic is forced through.

## Consequences
- Adding a new VPC becomes a single Transit Gateway attachment and route table association, not
  N peering operations against every existing VPC.
- All inter-VPC and egress traffic is inspectable at the single inspection VPC, satisfying the
  compliance team's centralized-logging requirement.
- The Transit Gateway becomes a single point of regional throughput contention and a per-region
  cost line item (data processing charges per GB transferred through it) that full mesh peering
  would not have incurred; we accept this and will monitor TGW data-processing cost as a
  capacity-planning metric.
- Cross-region traffic requires Transit Gateway peering between regions, which we have not yet
  load-tested at the latency this platform's workloads require -- flagged as a follow-up spike
  before the next region is added.
commonMistakes: Listing only the chosen option as 'Option 1' with no genuinely rejected alternatives
Writing a Context section that states the decision without explaining what made it necessary
Writing a Consequences section that lists only benefits, with no real cost or risk named
Omitting the Status field, leaving a reader unsure whether the ADR still reflects the current design
Writing an ADR as a full system design document instead of a record of one specific decision
keyPoints: ADR format: Context, Options Considered, Decision, Consequences
Options Considered must include real alternatives that were genuinely rejected, with why
Decision must be unambiguous, not hedged
Consequences must name a real downside/cost, not just the benefit
A Status field lets a future reader know if the ADR still reflects reality

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct four-section ADR structure
Context section correctly explains what made the decision necessary
At least two genuinely rejected alternatives with real reasons
Consequences section states a real downside, not just upside
Clarity and correct Transit Gateway technical content

questions.title: The Failover That Worked and the Outage That Didn't End
questions.prompt: A company's claims-processing database fails over to its secondary region exactly as designed, within its 2-hour RTO, during a 6-hour regional outage. Yet the full outage lasts nearly 11 hours, because almost nothing in the secondary region can actually serve traffic. Diagnose what actually went wrong given that every application-tier RTO/RPO target was met, and identify the one review-board question that would have caught this before it ever happened.
questions.modelAnswer:
The application tier did exactly what it was designed to do -- the database failed over within its RTO, as did the other application workloads. The actual failure is one level below the applications: the hub -- the shared Azure Firewall, VPN gateway, and DNS Private Resolver that every spoke depends on for egress and internal name resolution -- existed only in the primary region. It was never deployed to the secondary region, because no ADR, design document, or review item had ever framed shared network services as something needing its own disaster recovery plan; it was treated as background 'infrastructure,' not as a tier with its own RTO/RPO.

With the hub down, every spoke's outbound route -- the user-defined route pointing `0.0.0.0/0` at the firewall's private IP -- pointed at nothing. The failed-over database was healthy and reachable from inside its own spoke, but nothing could resolve internal DNS to find it, and nothing could reach the internet to serve the public-facing site. The actual time to restore service was dominated not by any application failing to fail over, but by the fact that nobody had asked whether the network being failed over into actually existed at all.

Three contributing factors combined into this blind spot: the review checklist was application-shaped (RTO/RPO per workload naturally produces a list of applications, and a shared network layer owned by no single team doesn't appear on that list unless someone explicitly adds it); ownership was ambiguous (the platform team built and operated the hub, but each application team wrote its own workload's DR plan, and neither side believed the hub's DR plan was their job); and the design diagram looked complete (a hub-and-spoke diagram with a secondary region drawn next to the primary implies symmetry that was never actually built).

The one review-board question that would have surfaced this: 'If the primary region's hub goes down, what happens to every spoke that depends on it for egress and DNS -- and is that dependency's own RTO/RPO documented anywhere?' That question forces the shared-services tier onto the same checklist as every application tier, instead of being implicitly assumed to just exist wherever it's needed.
questions.professionalAnswer: What's interesting about this one is that the application layer genuinely did everything right -- the database failed over inside its RTO, exactly as designed. The actual failure is one level down from that: the shared hub -- firewall, VPN gateway, DNS resolver -- only ever existed in the primary region, because nobody had ever written down that it needed its own DR plan. It was just 'infrastructure,' and infrastructure wasn't on anyone's RTO/RPO checklist. So when the hub went down, the failed-over database was perfectly healthy but completely unreachable -- nothing could resolve DNS to find it, nothing had an egress path. The time to fully restore service was really dominated by that gap, not by anything application-related failing to fail over. The one question that would've caught this ahead of time is simple: if the hub goes down, what happens to every spoke that depends on it, and is that dependency's own RTO/RPO written down anywhere? That forces the shared network layer onto the same checklist as every application, instead of being silently assumed to just exist.
commonMistakes: Concluding the failover 'worked' because the application tier met its RTO, missing that service wasn't actually restored
Treating this as an application-layer bug rather than a missing shared-services DR plan
Not identifying the review checklist's application-shaped structure as the real reason the gap was never surfaced
Assuming a diagram showing a secondary region means that region's shared services were actually deployed there
Failing to name the specific review-board question that would have caught the gap
keyPoints: Application tiers met their RTO/RPO; the actual failure was the undeployed shared network hub
The hub (firewall, VPN gateway, DNS resolver) existed only in the primary region
Without the hub, failed-over applications were healthy but unreachable (no DNS, no egress)
The checklist's application-shaped structure, ambiguous ownership, and diagram symmetry combined to hide this
The fix is one explicit review question treating shared network services as their own DR-in-scope tier

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the undeployed shared hub as the real root cause
Correctly explains why failed-over applications were still unreachable
Identifies the structural reasons the review missed this (checklist shape, ownership, diagram)
States the correct review-board question that would have caught it

questions.title: The Compliance Report That Said Everything Was Fine
questions.prompt: A security audit finds several S3 buckets in production accounts with public read access -- despite an AWS Config rule that's been 'checking for this' for over a year, with a dashboard showing 98% compliance. Explain exactly why a passing Config-rule dashboard didn't actually prevent this, what an SCP would have done differently, and the specific change you'd make to close the gap without just adding another dashboard nobody questions.
questions.modelAnswer:
The root confusion is treating an AWS Config rule as if it were a preventive control, when it's architecturally a detective one. A Config rule continuously evaluates resources that already exist against a rule and reports compliance -- it never stops a non-compliant resource from being created in the first place; its default behavior is detection, not prevention. A 98% compliance dashboard means the rule is correctly reporting that 2% of buckets are non-compliant -- it is working exactly as designed, and the dashboard being 'mostly green' is precisely what let this sit unnoticed, because 98% reads as a success metric rather than as 'some number of buckets are currently publicly readable right now.'

An SCP would have done something structurally different: attached to the Organizational Unit containing these production accounts, an SCP denying the specific actions that make a bucket public (for example denying `s3:PutBucketAcl` or `s3:PutBucketPolicy` calls that would set public access, or more directly using the account-level S3 Block Public Access settings enforced via SCP) sets a hard ceiling at the IAM/API level that applies to every identity in every account under that OU -- even the account's own root user can't exceed it. The bucket would never have become public in the first place, because the API call to make it public would be denied outright, not reported after the fact.

The fix isn't a new dashboard -- it's converting the specific, well-understood risk (public bucket access, which can be fully described as a rule: 'never allow this API call to succeed') from a detective control into a preventive one. Concretely: add or tighten an SCP at the OU level enforcing S3 Block Public Access settings and denying the relevant public-ACL/public-policy API calls, so this specific category of mistake becomes structurally impossible rather than something a dashboard reports after it already happened. The Config rule still has value for anything that genuinely can't be reduced to a hard API-level rule, or as a defense-in-depth backstop, but it should not have been the only control standing between 'someone configures this wrong' and 'this becomes publicly readable.'
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I'd want to correct first is the assumption that a Config rule was ever supposed to prevent this. It's a detective control -- it checks resources that already exist and reports on them, it never stops the bucket from becoming public in the first place. A 98% compliance number actually means 2% of buckets are confirmed public right now, which reads like a success metric but really isn't one. An SCP would do something structurally different -- attached at the OU level, denying the specific API calls that make a bucket public, it applies to every identity in every account under it, even the root user, so the bucket would never have gone public to begin with, because the call itself gets denied. So the fix isn't a better dashboard, it's converting this specific, well-understood risk into a preventive control -- an SCP enforcing block-public-access and denying the relevant ACL/policy calls -- and keeping the Config rule around as a backstop for whatever the SCP doesn't fully cover.
commonMistakes: Treating a passing Config-rule dashboard as proof the risk was actually prevented
Not recognizing Config rules as detective controls versus SCPs as preventive controls
Proposing another report or dashboard rather than a structural, API-level denial
Missing that an SCP applies even against the account's own root user, which a Config rule finding doesn't
Suggesting the Config rule should be removed entirely rather than kept as a complementary backstop
keyPoints: AWS Config rules are detective controls: they report on resources that already exist, never prevent creation
A 98% compliance dashboard means some resources are confirmed non-compliant, which is a risk, not a success
SCPs are preventive controls at the IAM/API layer, applying to every identity in every account under an OU
The actual fix is an SCP denying the specific public-access API calls, not a better dashboard
A mature governance design uses both: SCPs to make the worst mistakes impossible, Config rules as a backstop

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses Config rules as detective, not preventive
Correctly explains why a 98% dashboard masked a real ongoing risk
Correctly explains what an SCP would do differently (API-level denial)
Proposes the correct concrete fix rather than more reporting

questions.title: Drawing Account Boundaries for a Company That Reorgs Constantly
questions.prompt: A company wants a new multi-account structure and proposes 'one subscription per department, matching the org chart, so it's obvious who owns what.' The company also reorganizes its engineering teams roughly twice a year. Explain exactly why the org-chart proposal is the wrong design, what should replace it as the deciding logic, and design the account boundaries for a concrete scenario: a payments team running a production database, a low-stakes internal wiki, and a bursty nightly batch job, all currently under one department.
questions.modelAnswer:
Org-chart mirroring fails for a structural reason, not a stylistic one: an org chart describes who reports to whom, not what should blow up together. A reorg that moves engineers between departments has nothing to do with whether their workloads should still share an account, yet an org-chart-mapped boundary forces someone to redraw the cloud structure every time the people structure changes -- and this company reorganizes twice a year, which means this proposal guarantees a recurring, unnecessary redesign project. Worse, a department-sized boundary is the wrong size in both directions at once here: it's too coarse to separate the payments team's genuinely risky production database from its low-stakes internal wiki (both would end up in the same 'Payments' subscription), and too fine to let a security boundary span exactly the resources that actually need to share one.

The deciding logic that should replace it is blast radius: if this one account were fully compromised, misconfigured, or hit a hard provider limit, what's the worst case -- and is that worst case something the organization is willing to tolerate from a single incident? That reframes the decision from an org-chart lookup into an actual risk calculation, evaluated across four dimensions: security blast radius, compliance/regulatory scope, billing/cost isolation, and operational access.

Applied to the concrete scenario: the production database gets its own boundary, isolated specifically from everything else in the department, because a compromised credential or a bad deployment anywhere else should never have a network or IAM path to it -- production versus non-production is the boundary almost every real design draws first. The internal wiki is low-stakes and low-risk; it can sit in a separate, shared non-production or internal-tools subscription with other similarly low-risk workloads from other teams, since there's no meaningful blast-radius argument for isolating it specifically by department. The bursty nightly batch job gets its own boundary primarily for billing isolation -- its volatile, spiky cost would otherwise drown out visibility into the payments team's steady-state budget, and a dedicated boundary gives it a clean, separate chargeback line independent of who happens to own it organizationally.

The result is three different boundaries for what the org chart would have called 'one department's cloud footprint' -- which is exactly the point: the boundaries reflect what should blow up together and what should be billed separately, not who reports to whom, and none of them need to be redrawn the next time this company reorganizes.
questions.professionalAnswer: My pushback on 'one subscription per department' is pretty direct: an org chart tells you who reports to whom, not what should blow up together, and this company reorgs twice a year, so that proposal guarantees redrawing the cloud structure on a schedule that has nothing to do with risk. I'd reframe the actual question as blast radius -- if this one account got fully compromised or hit a hard limit, what's the worst case, and is that tolerable? For the scenario given, I'd split it three ways: the production database gets its own isolated boundary, full stop, because nothing else should have a path to it regardless of who owns it. The wiki is genuinely low risk, so it can sit in a shared non-production or internal-tools subscription with other low-stakes stuff. And the batch job gets its own boundary mainly for billing reasons -- its spiky cost would otherwise drown out visibility into the team's steady-state budget. None of those three boundaries need to move the next time this company reorganizes.
commonMistakes: Accepting 'one subscription per department' because it looks organizationally tidy
Not connecting the reorg frequency directly to why org-chart boundaries are a recurring maintenance cost
Putting the production database and the low-stakes wiki in the same boundary because they share a department
Missing billing/cost isolation as a legitimate, separate reason to carve out the batch job
Proposing either one account for everything or one account per team, the two anti-patterns with the same root cause
keyPoints: Org-chart mirroring forces a cloud redesign every time the org chart changes
Blast radius -- the worst case if this boundary is fully compromised -- is the correct deciding question
Four real dimensions drive the line: security blast radius, compliance scope, billing isolation, operational access
Production should be isolated from non-production regardless of which team owns both
A volatile-cost workload (the batch job) deserves its own billing boundary independent of org ownership

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why org-chart mirroring fails, tied to the reorg frequency
Correctly proposes blast radius as the deciding question
Correctly isolates the production database as its own boundary
Correctly reasons about the wiki and batch job using the right dimensions (risk vs. billing)
Clarity

questions.title: Designing Network Connectivity for 50 Teams on Two Clouds
questions.prompt: A platform currently has 8 application teams on Azure, each VNet directly peered to the ones it needs to reach, and is about to onboard 42 more teams, split across Azure and a new AWS presence. Design the real network topology for this growth, explaining specifically why the current approach breaks, how Azure and AWS each solve the resulting problem, and what you'd reach for once hand-wiring the Azure side stops being maintainable.
questions.modelAnswer:
Direct VNet-to-VNet peering is a full mesh, and a full mesh's connection count grows roughly as N² against the number of networks. At 8 teams that's tolerable; growing to 50 means potentially over a thousand peering relationships, each needing its own route and firewall review -- an unmanageable tangle, and exactly the problem hub-and-spoke exists to solve.

On the Azure side, the fix is hub-and-spoke built from VNet peering plus user-defined routes, and the one fact that makes it work is that VNet peering is explicitly non-transitive: if spoke A and spoke B both peer with the hub, A cannot reach B through the hub automatically. That's the feature, not a limitation -- it forces the hub to be the only path, enforced by giving each spoke subnet a route table whose default route (`0.0.0.0/0`) points at the hub's firewall or NVA instead of straight to the internet. The connection count drops to roughly N, and every cross-network packet now passes one chokepoint where a single policy applies instead of fifty. Once the number of spokes (or regions) makes hand-maintaining a UDR on every spoke subnet too error-prone -- and at 50 teams across two regions, this is exactly that point -- the right move is Azure Virtual WAN, a Microsoft-managed hub that replaces hand-built hub VNets and manually maintained UDRs with the same architectural intent, managed by the platform instead of wired by hand.

On the new AWS side, AWS Transit Gateway is the direct analog: a single, AWS-managed regional router that VPCs, VPNs, and Direct Connect links attach to. Where Azure needs a UDR per spoke subnet to force traffic toward a hub NVA, Transit Gateway handles routing natively -- each VPC attachment associates with a transit gateway route table, which decides what it can reach, making it straightforward to force everything through a dedicated inspection VPC or isolate a sensitive VPC to only the shared-services attachment.

The architectural intent is identical on both clouds -- one shared connection point, centralized policy enforcement, linear rather than quadratic connection growth -- but Azure trades more of that onto the architect (hand-built UDRs, until Virtual WAN takes it over) while Transit Gateway manages the transitive routing natively from day one. For this specific growth -- going from 8 to 50 teams across two clouds -- I'd move the Azure side onto Virtual WAN at the same time the AWS side stands up Transit Gateway, rather than scaling the hand-built UDR approach to 42 new spokes and hitting the maintainability wall almost immediately after onboarding them.
questions.professionalAnswer: Going from 8 teams to 50 across two clouds, I'd flag immediately that straight peering stops being viable -- full mesh grows roughly with the square of the number of networks, so a thousand-plus peering relationships just isn't something anyone's reviewing by hand. On the Azure side, hub-and-spoke works because VNet peering is explicitly non-transitive -- that's the feature, not a limitation -- enforced with UDRs pointing every spoke's default route at the hub's firewall. On AWS, Transit Gateway gets you the same outcome natively, with route table associations deciding what each attachment can reach instead of hand-maintained routes. The real answer to 'what do you reach for' is: once hand-wiring UDRs across that many Azure spokes gets too error-prone to trust, which at 50 teams it will, you move to Virtual WAN, which is Microsoft's managed version of the same idea -- basically Azure's closer analog to what Transit Gateway already gives you on day one.
commonMistakes: Proposing to keep scaling direct peering past the point where connection count becomes unmanageable
Not identifying VNet peering's non-transitivity as the specific mechanism that makes hub-and-spoke work
Treating Azure Virtual WAN and AWS Transit Gateway as unrelated rather than the same architectural intent on two clouds
Missing that the trigger for moving to Virtual WAN is specifically when hand-maintained UDRs become too error-prone, not a fixed team count
Forgetting that Transit Gateway's route tables are what enforces 'no direct spoke-to-spoke' on AWS, the way UDRs do on Azure
keyPoints: Full mesh peering grows quadratically; hub-and-spoke/Transit Gateway reduces it to roughly linear
Azure VNet peering's non-transitivity, enforced via UDRs, is what forces traffic through the hub
AWS Transit Gateway natively handles transitive routing via route table associations
Azure Virtual WAN is the managed-hub answer once hand-built UDRs stop scaling
The architectural intent (one chokepoint, centralized policy) is identical across both clouds

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why full mesh peering breaks at this scale
Correctly explains Azure hub-and-spoke mechanics (non-transitive peering plus UDRs)
Correctly explains AWS Transit Gateway mechanics
Correctly identifies when/why to move to Virtual WAN
Clarity

questions.title: Letting RTO and RPO Pick the DR Pattern, Not the Other Way Around
questions.prompt: Two workloads need a disaster recovery design: a financial ledger (RTO of 4 hours is acceptable, but RPO must be effectively zero -- losing even a minute of transactions is unacceptable) and a read-heavy marketing content site (RTO must be under a minute, but RPO of an hour is fine). Design the DR architecture for each, explain why picking 'active-active everywhere' or 'active-passive everywhere' as a blanket policy would be wrong for at least one of them, and justify each choice strictly from the stated RTO/RPO numbers.
questions.modelAnswer:
These two workloads have inverted requirements, which is exactly why a single blanket DR policy would fail one of them.

The financial ledger's RPO of effectively zero means only continuous, synchronous replication meets the bar -- the secondary copy has to be updated as writes happen, not on any schedule, because even a few seconds of data loss is unacceptable for a transaction history. Its RTO of 4 hours, though, is loose: infrastructure doesn't need to already be running and absorbing traffic. This maps to active-passive with synchronous replication to a warm or even cold/pilot-light standby -- the data layer stays continuously current (meeting the zero-RPO bar), while compute can be provisioned from Infrastructure as Code and scaled up only after a disaster is declared, comfortably inside a 4-hour window. Active-active would be the wrong choice here specifically because it adds multi-master write-conflict resolution complexity and doubles running cost to chase an RTO target (seconds) that was never required -- the ledger's actual constraint is RPO, not RTO, and active-passive with synchronous replication already satisfies RPO without paying for active-active's conflict-resolution problem at all.

The marketing content site's RTO of under a minute rules out active-passive entirely, regardless of standby tier -- DNS propagation and any data-store promotion step alone will blow past a sub-minute target, even with a hot standby, because 'promote the standby' is itself a step with latency. Its RPO of an hour is loose, which is good news, because it means the read-heavy content doesn't need synchronous cross-region writes at all -- active-active with asynchronous or eventually-consistent replication, behind global traffic distribution (DNS-based routing or a global load balancer), gets failover down to essentially a traffic-rerouting operation measured in seconds, satisfying the RTO, while the hour-long RPO tolerance means occasional replication lag on writes is a non-issue for this workload.

A blanket 'active-active everywhere' policy would force the ledger into unnecessary multi-master write-conflict engineering it doesn't need to meet its actual target. A blanket 'active-passive everywhere' policy would make the content site's sub-minute RTO structurally unachievable, no matter how the standby is tiered. Both targets have to drive the pattern independently, workload by workload, because they point to genuinely opposite answers here.
questions.professionalAnswer: These two workloads are basically mirror images of each other, which is what makes this a good test of whether you're actually using RTO and RPO or just picking a pattern you like. The ledger's real constraint is RPO -- it can't lose even a minute of transactions -- so it needs synchronous replication, but its RTO is loose enough that the compute side can just be a warm or even cold standby, provisioned from code after a disaster's declared. Active-active would be overkill here; you'd be taking on multi-master conflict resolution to chase an RTO nobody asked for. The content site is the opposite -- its RTO is under a minute, which no active-passive standby tier can hit, because promoting a standby and waiting on DNS alone blows past that. Its RPO is loose, though, so active-active with async replication is actually the cheaper, simpler fit there, not the more expensive one. A single company-wide DR policy would get at least one of these wrong no matter which pattern it picked.
commonMistakes: Picking one DR pattern as a company-wide standard rather than deriving it per workload from RTO/RPO
Choosing active-active for the ledger because 'more resilient sounds better,' missing that RPO, not RTO, is its real constraint
Choosing active-passive for the content site without checking whether any standby tier can meet a sub-minute RTO
Confusing RTO and RPO as the same concept, or assuming one number implies the other
Not naming the specific mechanism (synchronous replication, hot/warm/cold standby tier) that makes each choice actually meet its target
keyPoints: RPO drives backup/replication strategy; RTO drives standby capacity -- they're independent axes
The ledger's zero RPO requires synchronous replication; its loose RTO allows a cheap standby tier
The content site's sub-minute RTO requires active-active; its loose RPO allows async replication
A blanket single-pattern policy fails whichever workload's actual constraint doesn't match that pattern's strength
Each choice should be justified strictly from the stated numbers, not from a general preference for one pattern

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs the ledger's DR architecture from its RPO/RTO numbers
Correctly designs the content site's DR architecture from its RPO/RTO numbers
Correctly explains why blanket active-active fails the ledger
Correctly explains why blanket active-passive fails the content site

questions.title: Designing Governance So Teams Stop Routing Around It
questions.prompt: A platform team notices application teams increasingly provisioning resources manually outside the sanctioned pipeline, because getting anything approved through the current change advisory board takes two weeks regardless of risk. Redesign the governance model using the guardrail-vs-gate distinction: classify which current approval requirements should become automated guardrails, which genuinely need to stay as human gates, and explain the specific test you'd apply to make that call.
questions.modelAnswer:
The shadow-IT behavior described -- teams provisioning manually outside the pipeline -- is the predictable result of defaulting to gates for everything: when getting a routine, low-risk resource approved takes the same two-week cycle as a genuinely novel, high-consequence change, teams learn that the sanctioned path is slower than the problem it's solving and route around it. The fix isn't removing governance, it's redistributing which risks are enforced as guardrails (automated, preventive, no human in the loop, holding even at 2 a.m. with nobody awake) versus gates (a human explicitly reviewing and approving a specific change before it proceeds).

The test to apply to any current approval requirement: could this risk be fully described as a rule a machine can check? If the actual concern reduces to 'don't do X without Y configured' -- allowed regions, required tags, encryption settings, instance size limits, public-access restrictions -- it should be a policy (an Azure Policy `Deny` assignment, an AWS SCP, a Terraform pipeline check), not a meeting. If the risk is genuinely novel, high-consequence, and resistant to being reduced to a checklist -- a first-of-its-kind data-sharing arrangement with an external partner, an architecture decision with real compliance exposure that's never been reviewed before, an irreversible and expensive-to-undo action -- it stays a gate, because the entire point of a gate is a human judgment call on something that can't be fully encoded as a rule.

Applied concretely: routine resource provisioning within approved regions, instance sizes, and tagging requirements converts to guardrails -- policy as code shipped through the same pipeline as the infrastructure it governs, so a team deploying at 2 a.m. finds out immediately if something's non-compliant, the same fast feedback loop as a compiler error, instead of waiting three days for a review meeting. A production database migration, a new public-facing endpoint with real security exposure, or a change above a significant cost threshold stays a gate, because each of those is a case where a human genuinely needs to exercise judgment that can't be reduced to a checklist today.

The reason this redesign actually stops the shadow-IT behavior, rather than just being a different policy document: guardrails don't cost a compliant team any time at all -- a team that follows the rules never notices the guardrail is there -- so routine work stops needing to wait in the same queue as the genuinely risky decisions that still deserve a gate's scrutiny.
questions.professionalAnswer: What I'd point out first is that the shadow-IT behavior described is exactly what you'd expect when every approval, regardless of actual risk, goes through the same two-week gate -- teams learn the sanctioned path is slower than the problem it's solving, so they go around it. My fix wouldn't be to speed up the gate, it'd be to shrink what actually needs one. The test I'd apply to every current approval: can this be fully written as a rule a machine checks? Region restrictions, required tags, encryption settings, instance sizes -- all of that becomes a guardrail, shipped as policy as code, so a compliant team never even notices it's there. What stays a gate is the stuff that's genuinely novel or irreversible -- a first-of-its-kind data-sharing deal, an architecture decision with real compliance exposure nobody's reviewed before. The reason this actually stops the routing-around behavior, rather than just being a different policy doc, is that guardrails cost a compliant team zero time -- it's only the genuinely risky stuff left waiting on a human.
commonMistakes: Proposing to simply speed up the existing gate process rather than converting most routine risks into guardrails
Treating 'guardrails are good, gates are bad' rather than matching each risk to the right mechanism
Classifying a risk as a gate without first testing whether it could actually be written as a machine-checkable rule
Not identifying the specific examples of what should stay a gate (novel, high-consequence, irreversible decisions)
Missing the causal link between defaulting to gates and the shadow-IT behavior already described in the prompt
keyPoints: Defaulting to gates for everything is what produces the shadow-IT behavior described
The test: could this risk be fully described as a rule a machine can check?
Routine, rule-describable risks (regions, tags, sizes, encryption) become automated guardrails
Genuinely novel, high-consequence, irreversible decisions stay as human gates
Guardrails cost a compliant team no time, which is what actually stops the routing-around behavior

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses why defaulting to gates caused the shadow-IT behavior
States and applies the correct guardrail-vs-gate test
Correctly classifies concrete examples into guardrails vs. gates
Explains why the redesign actually stops the routing-around behavior

questions.title: Defending a Tradeoff You Made on Purpose
questions.prompt: You're presenting your architecture to a review board. You deliberately chose not to build cross-region failover for a non-critical internal reporting service, to hit a launch deadline. A board member pushes back: 'This has no disaster recovery story at all -- that seems like a real gap.' Walk through exactly how you'd respond, using the real three-part pattern for defending a deliberate tradeoff, and contrast it with how this would go if you got defensive instead.
questions.modelAnswer:
The key distinction to establish immediately is that this is a decision, not a gap -- 'we didn't think about failover' and 'we chose not to build failover because the service is non-critical and the engineering cost didn't justify it' describe the same technical fact but are completely different things to say in a review, and the board member's question deserves to hear which one this actually is.

I'd use the three-part pattern directly. First, restate the constraint that drove the decision: 'We were optimizing for a hard launch date on a service that's internal-only and non-revenue-facing.' This reframes the conversation from 'is this defensible in isolation' to 'given this real constraint, was this a reasonable call' -- the question the board actually wants answered. Second, name the alternative and its specific cost: 'We could have built active-active failover across two regions, which would have added roughly 40% to this service's infrastructure cost and several weeks of engineering time we didn't have before launch, for a workload with no formal availability target and no revenue impact if it's down for a few hours.' Concrete numbers here show I considered the more resilient option and had a specific reason to reject it, not that I was unaware it existed. Third, invite the counter-proposal: 'If this service's criticality has changed since we made this call -- if it's now feeding something customer-facing, for instance -- I want to hear that, because the decision was based on a specific set of constraints that might not hold anymore.'

If I got defensive instead -- treating the question as an attack, relitigating every option I considered live instead of stating the one reason that mattered, or immediately conceding to 'reconsider' just to end the discomfort -- a sound decision would look weak in the room even though nothing about the underlying tradeoff changed. Conceding everything isn't collaboration; it trains the board to treat every deliberate tradeoff as negotiable, which undermines the next one I present. Being collaborative means engaging with genuinely new information if it's actually offered, not abandoning a reasoned decision just because it was questioned -- a question is not automatically evidence the decision was wrong.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd want to make really clear, right away, that this wasn't an oversight -- it was a call we made on purpose, and I'd say so directly instead of getting defensive about it. I'd start with the constraint: we had a hard launch date and this is an internal tool, not customer-facing, no revenue tied to it being down for a few hours. Then I'd name what the alternative actually would have cost -- something like, building real cross-region failover here would've added maybe 40% to the infra bill for this service and pushed the timeline out by weeks, for a workload that doesn't have an availability target anyone's asked for. And I'd close by genuinely inviting the pushback to go somewhere useful -- if this thing's scope has changed, if it's suddenly feeding something customer-facing, I want to know that, because the call I made was based on a specific situation that might not be true anymore. What I wouldn't do is immediately say 'yeah, you're right, let's add it' just to make the question go away -- that doesn't actually serve anyone, it just means the next time I make a deliberate tradeoff, the room assumes it's up for grabs too.
commonMistakes: Treating the pushback as an attack and becoming defensive
Relitigating every option considered from scratch instead of stating the one deciding reason
Conceding to 'reconsider' immediately just to end the discomfort of being questioned
Failing to distinguish, out loud, between a gap and a deliberate decision
Not giving concrete numbers for the rejected alternative's cost, leaving the defense vague
keyPoints: Distinguish explicitly between a gap and a deliberate decision -- the board can't tell from the diagram alone
Restate the real constraint that drove the decision first
Name the rejected alternative and its specific, concrete cost
Invite a counter-proposal rather than defending the decision as permanently closed
Avoid both defensiveness and reflexive concession, which both weaken a sound decision in the room

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly frames this as a deliberate decision, not a gap
Correctly applies the constraint step of the three-part pattern
Correctly applies the alternative-and-cost step with concrete numbers
Correctly applies the counter-proposal invitation
Contrasts with the defensive/over-conceding failure modes

questions.title: Preparing for a Review Board You Can't Fully Predict
questions.prompt: You're three days out from presenting a new platform architecture to a review board for the first time. You've built real RTO/RPO numbers and a cost projection, but you're nervous because you genuinely don't know what they'll ask. Walk through how you'd actually prepare, using the real categories of questions a review board almost always asks, and describe specifically how you'd handle it if your honest answer to one of them is unflattering.
questions.modelAnswer:
The anxiety usually comes from treating the board's questions as unpredictable, when in practice an experienced reviewer's questions cluster into a small number of recurring categories, because their job is to probe the same handful of failure classes in every design they review -- learning the categories is most of what 'being prepared' actually means.

I'd walk in having already answered, for my own design, the four categories that cover almost everything: 'What happens when X fails?' -- I'd pick the component most likely to fail (the database, the single region, a third-party dependency) and have a specific answer ready, run as my own pre-mortem out loud with my team before the real review, not discovered live in the room. 'What does this cost at 10x scale?' -- I'd know the unit economics cold: marginal cost per request or per user, and specifically whether that cost scales linearly or has a cliff (a tier boundary, an egress charge, a licensing seat count), because designs that look fine at pilot scale often hide a cost curve that bends badly. 'What's the security blast radius?' -- I'd know exactly what's reachable if one component is compromised, tied directly to the account and network boundaries in the design. 'What's the simplest version of this?' -- I'd prepare a real answer, not a defensive one, because this is usually a sincere operational question about ongoing maintenance cost, and a good answer specifically describes what the simpler version would give up and why that tradeoff wasn't the one made.

For anything I can't fully predict, I'd have two or three appendix slides ready for likely deep-dive questions -- a detailed cost breakdown, a subnet-level network diagram -- kept out of the main deck so the presentation stays tight but the answer is one click away if asked.

If my honest answer to one of these is unflattering -- say, the true answer to 'what happens when the database fails' really is 'the whole system goes down' -- I wouldn't hide that question or hope it doesn't come up. I'd either fix it before the review if there's time, or walk in ready to name it directly as an accepted risk with a stated reason: what the mitigation plan is, why that risk was accepted given the constraints, and what would change the calculus. An honest 'here's the gap and here's why we accepted it for now' is a far stronger position in that room than being caught flat-footed by a question I should have already asked myself.
questions.professionalAnswer: Honestly, most of my prep isn't about guessing exactly what they'll ask -- it's accepting that review boards ask the same handful of question types every time, just about different designs. So I run my own version of the meeting first: I sit with my team and ask, out loud, what happens when our most fragile piece fails, what this costs if we're suddenly at ten times the traffic, what's actually reachable if one piece gets compromised, and what the simplest version of this would look like and give up. If I've already had that conversation with myself, nothing in the real room is actually new, even if the specific wording of the question is. The part I used to get wrong is panicking when my own honest answer to one of those is bad -- like, yeah, if the database goes down right now, the whole thing goes down. I don't try to bury that. I either fix it before the meeting if I can, or I walk in and just say it plainly -- here's the gap, here's why we accepted it given our timeline, here's what we'd need to see to revisit it. That's a much stronger position than getting asked that question cold and fumbling it.
commonMistakes: Treating review board questions as fundamentally unpredictable rather than clustering into known categories
Not running a pre-mortem on your own design before the real review
Not knowing unit economics/cost-at-scale numbers cold
Hiding or hoping an unflattering answer doesn't come up instead of naming it as an accepted, reasoned risk
Treating 'what's the simplest version of this' as an attack rather than a sincere operational question deserving a real answer

Prepare appendix material for deep-dive questions without bloating the main deck

questions.title: Push vs. Pull-Based Deployment: The Security Case for GitOps
questions.prompt: Your team currently ships to a production Kubernetes cluster the conventional way: a GitHub Actions job runs `az aks get-credentials` and then `kubectl apply -f k8s/production/` at the end of every pipeline run. A newer engineer asks why the platform team wants to migrate this to ArgoCD instead of just tightening the existing pipeline's permissions. Explain exactly what credential the current pipeline has to hold and why that's a structural security liability, how a pull-based GitOps agent inverts the direction of trust, and which OpenGitOps principle formalizes the model you're recommending.
questions.modelAnswer:
The current pipeline is push-based: the CI runner authenticates outward to the cluster's API server and applies manifests directly, which means it has to hold a kubeconfig scoped to whatever `kubectl apply` needs to touch in production -- often a cluster-admin-grade credential, because most teams never get around to scoping per-pipeline, per-namespace permissions tightly. That credential sits as an encrypted secret in the CI system's configuration and gets decrypted into the runner's memory on every single run. Tightening the pipeline's own permissions narrows the blast radius a little, but it doesn't remove the structural problem: an external system still holds standing, privileged access to production, and the cluster's API server still has to accept inbound connections from wherever that runner happens to execute, which usually means it can't sit purely behind a private network with no exposed administrative ingress.

A pull-based GitOps agent -- ArgoCD or Flux, running inside the cluster -- inverts that relationship entirely. The agent authenticates outbound to Git using a read-only deploy key or scoped token, and applies changes using its own in-cluster RBAC permissions, which you can scope as tightly as any other Kubernetes Role. No external system -- not CI, not a laptop, not a human -- ever holds a privileged cluster credential, because the pipeline's job shrinks to building, testing, and committing a change to Git. If an attacker compromises the CI system entirely, there's no cluster-admin kubeconfig sitting in it to steal, because it was never issued one in the first place. The agent decides, on its own schedule or in response to a webhook, when to pull and apply -- the cluster reaches out, nothing reaches in.

This is exactly what OpenGitOps calls the 'Pulled Automatically' principle: software agents, not external pipelines, are responsible for pulling desired state from the source and applying it. The distinction the engineer should walk away with is that this isn't a tooling preference -- it's a different trust model that eliminates an entire class of credential, rather than trying to lock an inherently risky one down further.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Honestly the way I'd put it to a newer engineer is: tightening permissions on the existing pipeline is polishing a design that's wrong at the root, not fixing the actual problem. Right now that GitHub Actions job is fetching a real kubeconfig for production and running kubectl against it directly -- so somewhere in our CI secrets there's a credential that can modify prod, and it gets pulled into a runner's memory every time the pipeline fires. I've seen that go wrong before -- a poisoned dependency in a build step, or just a leaked secret, and suddenly whoever got in has whatever that runner's kubeconfig can touch.

What I like about moving to ArgoCD is it flips who's reaching for who. Instead of CI reaching into the cluster, you've got an agent sitting inside the cluster reaching out to Git, with its own scoped RBAC, and Git access that's read-only. So even in a worst-case CI compromise, there's nothing privileged to steal -- the pipeline literally never had cluster credentials. I'd tell the engineer that's the actual OpenGitOps idea behind 'pulled automatically' -- it's not just jargon, it's describing exactly that inversion, and it's the reason platform teams push for this migration instead of just adding more guardrails to the push model.
commonMistakes: Treating this as a permissions-scoping problem rather than a structural trust-model problem
Assuming the CI credential is only used for one app's namespace when in practice it's rarely scoped that tightly
Forgetting that the push model also forces the API server to accept inbound connections from wherever CI runs
Not naming the specific OpenGitOps principle (Pulled Automatically) when asked for it
Confusing 'pull-based' with 'the pipeline polls more often' instead of 'an in-cluster agent, not the pipeline, does the applying'
keyPoints: Push model: CI authenticates outward and holds a privileged kubeconfig
That credential is a standing, high-value target independent of any specific breach
Push also forces the API server to accept inbound connections from CI's network
Pull model: an in-cluster agent (ArgoCD/Flux) authenticates outbound to Git with read-only credentials
The agent applies changes using its own in-cluster RBAC, never an external cluster-admin credential
This is the OpenGitOps 'Pulled Automatically' principle

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the privileged kubeconfig credential in the push model
Explains why that credential is a structural liability, not just a scoping issue
Correctly describes how the pull-based agent inverts trust direction
Names the OpenGitOps Pulled Automatically principle
Clear, accurate, well-organized overall explanation

questions.title: Writing a Dev-to-Prod Promotion PR Without Rebuilding the Image
questions.prompt: Your org uses a directory-per-environment GitOps repo (`base/` plus `overlays/dev`, `overlays/staging`, `overlays/prod`, each with its own `kustomization.yaml` patching the image tag and replica count). CI just built and pushed `payments-api:7f3a9c1` after a merge to main, and it's already deployed cleanly to dev. Write the exact change you'd make to promote that build to staging, and then to prod, without ever rebuilding the image. Then explain what the diff of each promotion PR should -- and should not -- contain, and what you'd do differently if someone proposed rebuilding from source for the staging and prod deploys instead.
questions.code:
# overlays/dev/kustomization.yaml (already updated, deployed cleanly)
resources:
  - ../../base
images:
  - name: payments-api
    newTag: 7f3a9c1

# overlays/staging/kustomization.yaml (currently pointing at the previous build)
resources:
  - ../../base
images:
  - name: payments-api
    newTag: 4b1e02a
questions.modelAnswer:
Promotion means editing exactly one line in each next-environment overlay -- the image tag -- never the base, and never rebuilding anything. For staging, the change is a PR that sets `overlays/staging/kustomization.yaml`'s `images.newTag` from `4b1e02a` to `7f3a9c1`, identical to the SHA already running cleanly in dev. Once staging validation passes (automated tests plus whatever manual QA the team requires), a second promotion PR makes the same one-line change in `overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml`, this time usually gated by required reviewers or a change-management approval since it's the PR that actually changes what customers see.

The diff of each promotion PR should contain nothing but that tag value moving forward -- no replica count changes, no resource limit tweaks, no unrelated config edits bundled in. If a reviewer sees anything else in a promotion PR's diff, that's a signal the PR is doing two jobs at once and should be split, because it muddies exactly what's being promoted and makes a later `git revert` less safe. The PR should also never touch `base/`, since base is environment-agnostic by design; a change that needs to land in base belongs in its own PR, reviewed on its own merits, not smuggled in alongside a tag bump.

If someone proposed rebuilding from source for staging and prod instead of promoting the same artifact, I'd push back hard: rebuilding reopens exactly the bug class GitOps promotion exists to close. 'It worked in dev' stops meaning anything once staging's build and prod's build aren't provably the same bytes -- a different cached base-image layer, a dependency that silently resolved to a newer patch version, a build flag left on by accident. Once I'd want to know why someone even has the ability to rebuild from source at the staging/prod stage at all, since in a correctly designed pipeline those stages should only ever receive an already-built, already-immutable tag to promote.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd just open the PR and show the diff, honestly, because that's the whole argument. For staging, I'm editing one field -- `newTag` in `overlays/staging/kustomization.yaml` -- and setting it to the exact same SHA, `7f3a9c1`, that's already running in dev. Nothing else in that file changes. I usually script this with `kustomize edit set image` or a small `yq` one-liner so a human's only job is reviewing the diff, not typing a hash by hand and risking a typo. Once staging's had its validation pass, same move again for prod -- one line, same tag, usually with a couple of required reviewers on that PR because it's the one that actually ships to customers.

What I'd flag immediately if someone suggested rebuilding for staging or prod is: then what was the point of testing in staging at all? If prod's build isn't bit-for-bit the same artifact that passed in staging, you've thrown away the actual guarantee staging was supposed to give you. I've been burned by exactly this -- a dependency resolving to a different patch version between builds -- and it's a nasty one to debug because everyone assumes 'it was tested' when it really wasn't, not the version that shipped. So my answer there is: promote the tag, don't ever let staging or prod rebuild from source, full stop.
questions.example:
# overlays/staging/kustomization.yaml -- after the promotion PR merges
resources:
  - ../../base
images:
  - name: payments-api
    newTag: 7f3a9c1   # identical tag, copied from dev, not re-tagged

# the promotion PR's diff, in full:
#   - newTag: 4b1e02a
#   + newTag: 7f3a9c1

# scripted instead of hand-typed:
cd overlays/staging && kustomize edit set image payments-api=payments-api:7f3a9c1
commonMistakes: Rebuilding the image for staging or prod instead of promoting the already-built tag
Editing base/ to change the tag instead of the environment-specific overlay
Bundling unrelated config changes into the same promotion PR as the tag bump
Promoting to prod before staging validation has actually completed
Typing the tag by hand instead of scripting the edit, risking a mismatched SHA
Skipping required reviewers on the prod promotion PR because 'it's just a tag change'
keyPoints: The same immutable tag/digest moves unchanged through dev, staging, and prod
Only the overlay's image reference changes between environments, never base/
A promotion PR's diff should be a single line: the tag value
Prod promotion is gated behind staging validation and usually required reviewers
Rebuilding per environment reopens the 'it worked in staging' bug class GitOps promotion closes
Scripting the tag edit (kustomize edit set image, or yq) avoids hand-typed SHA mistakes
Rollback is a git revert of the promotion commit, not a manual kubectl command

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly edits only the target overlay's image tag, not base/
Correctly sequences dev -> staging validation -> prod promotion
Describes what the promotion PR diff should and should not contain
Correctly explains why rebuilding per environment is dangerous
Clear, technically accurate explanation overall

questions.title: Wiring an Automated Go/No-Go Signal into a Canary Rollout
questions.prompt: You're converting `checkout-service`'s plain Kubernetes `Deployment` into an Argo Rollouts `Rollout` with a canary strategy: 10% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100%, pausing 5 minutes at each step. Right now the pauses are just timers -- nothing is actually checking whether the canary is healthy before the rollout advances. Write the `AnalysisTemplate` that gates the rollout on error rate and p95 latency pulled from Prometheus, wire it into the `Rollout`'s canary steps, and explain exactly what happens -- to traffic and to the Git state -- if the analysis fails twice in a row.
questions.code:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata:
  name: checkout-service
spec:
  replicas: 10
  strategy:
    canary:
      steps:
        - setWeight: 10
        - pause: { duration: 5m }
        - setWeight: 25
        - pause: { duration: 5m }
        - setWeight: 50
        - pause: { duration: 10m }
        - setWeight: 100
questions.modelAnswer:
The pauses alone are just a timer -- nothing inspects whether the canary is actually healthy during them, so the rollout marches forward on a fixed schedule regardless of what's happening in production. Closing that gap means defining an `AnalysisTemplate` with a Prometheus query per signal, a `successCondition`, and a `failureLimit`, then referencing it from the `Rollout`'s `strategy.canary.analysis` block so each step is backed by a real check instead of a blind wait.

For checkout-service I'd watch two signals, not just one: error rate (5xx responses over total requests, scoped specifically to the canary revision) and p95 latency, because a version that's technically correct but twice as slow is still a regression a pure error-rate check would miss entirely. Both metrics live in the same `AnalysisTemplate`, each with its own threshold; a failure on either one counts toward `failureLimit`. The query has to filter on the canary's revision label specifically -- querying `http_requests_total{job="checkout"}` without a revision filter would blend canary and stable traffic together and mask a real regression in the small canary slice.

Wiring it in means adding an `analysis` block inside `strategy.canary` that references the template by name, with `startingStep` set so the check doesn't fire during the very first weight step while traffic is still settling. If the analysis fails twice consecutively (`failureLimit: 2`), Argo Rollouts aborts the rollout on its own: it scales the canary ReplicaSet down to zero, returns 100% of traffic to the last known-good stable revision, and reports the `Rollout` as `Degraded`. Critically, nothing about this is silent -- the Git commit that introduced the bad version is still sitting in the repo, and ArgoCD still shows that `Application` as reflecting a change that failed analysis, so the failure is fully visible and auditable, with no manual `kubectl rollback` and no human paged before the abort happened.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I always start by pointing out the gap in the plain version: a `pause` doesn't look at anything, it just waits, so if nobody's staring at a dashboard during that five minutes, a bad canary sails straight through to the next weight step. What fixes that is an `AnalysisTemplate` -- basically, a PromQL query plus a pass/fail rule that Argo Rollouts runs for you automatically at each step instead of a human watching Grafana.

For something customer-facing like checkout, I wouldn't ship with just an error-rate check -- I'd add p95 latency too, because I've seen a 'technically working' release that was just quietly slow, and pure error-rate monitoring would've waved it straight through. The thing I always double-check in these queries is that they're scoped to the canary's revision label specifically -- if you query across both canary and stable pods together, you can completely hide a regression that's only showing up in the small slice of traffic actually hitting the new version.

And on what happens if it fails -- that's actually my favorite part of this setup to explain, because it's fully automatic and fully visible. Two failed checks in a row, and the rollout just aborts itself: traffic snaps back to the stable version, the canary pods scale to zero, and I don't have to page anyone or run a rollback command. The only thing I do afterward is go look at the `Application` in ArgoCD -- it's sitting there `OutOfSync`, showing exactly which commit caused the abort, so there's a full paper trail even though nothing required a human in the loop while it happened.
questions.example:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AnalysisTemplate
metadata:
  name: checkout-canary-health
spec:
  metrics:
    - name: error-rate
      interval: 1m
      successCondition: result[0] <= 0.01
      failureLimit: 2
      provider:
        prometheus:
          address: http://prometheus.monitoring:9090
          query: |
            sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout",revision="canary",status=~"5.."}[5m]))
            /
            sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout",revision="canary"}[5m]))
    - name: p95-latency
      interval: 1m
      successCondition: result[0] <= 0.3
      failureLimit: 2
      provider:
        prometheus:
          address: http://prometheus.monitoring:9090
          query: |
            histogram_quantile(0.95,
              sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="checkout",revision="canary"}[5m])) by (le))
---
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata:
  name: checkout-service
spec:
  replicas: 10
  strategy:
    canary:
      analysis:
        templates:
          - templateName: checkout-canary-health
        startingStep: 2
      steps:
        - setWeight: 10
        - pause: { duration: 5m }
        - setWeight: 25
        - pause: { duration: 5m }
        - setWeight: 50
        - pause: { duration: 10m }
        - setWeight: 100
commonMistakes: Defining an AnalysisTemplate but forgetting to reference it inside strategy.canary.analysis, so it never actually runs
Checking only error rate and missing a latency regression that a correct-but-slow build would cause
Querying Prometheus without scoping to the canary revision label, blending canary and stable traffic together
Setting failureLimit too high, letting a real regression ride through on 'noise'
Omitting startingStep, so analysis fires during the very first weight step while metrics are still settling
Assuming the abort happens silently, when Git and ArgoCD both still show the failed commit as OutOfSync
keyPoints: AnalysisTemplate defines one or more metric queries with a successCondition and failureLimit
The template must be referenced inside strategy.canary.analysis.templates to actually run
Each query should be scoped specifically to the canary revision, not the whole service
Watching more than one signal (error rate and latency) catches regressions a single metric would miss
Failing the threshold failureLimit times in a row aborts the rollout automatically
An abort scales canary pods to zero and returns traffic to the last stable revision
The failed commit remains visible in Git and as OutOfSync in ArgoCD -- nothing disappears silently

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Writes a correct AnalysisTemplate with query, successCondition, and failureLimit
Correctly wires the template into the Rollout's canary analysis block
Scopes the Prometheus query to the canary revision specifically
Includes a second signal (e.g. latency) beyond error rate
Correctly explains the automated abort behavior and resulting Git/ArgoCD state

questions.title: Drift That Keeps Getting Reverted: Diagnosing a Fight With the Reconciler
questions.prompt: During a traffic spike last night, an on-call engineer ran `kubectl scale deployment payments-api --replicas=10` to add capacity. It worked immediately -- but roughly three minutes later, replicas dropped back to 5, and it's happened twice more since, each time the engineer rescales. The team is confused why their manual fix keeps disappearing. Diagnose exactly what's happening, name the ArgoCD setting responsible, and explain the correct way to make the capacity increase stick without turning off the behavior that's reverting it.
questions.code:
$ kubectl scale deployment payments-api --replicas=10
deployment.apps/payments-api scaled

# ~3 minutes later
$ kubectl get deployment payments-api
NAME           READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE
payments-api   5/5     5            5
questions.modelAnswer:
This isn't a flake -- it's the reconciler doing exactly what it's configured to do. The `payments-api` `Application` has `syncPolicy.automated.selfHeal: true`, which means ArgoCD continuously diffs live cluster state against what's declared in Git, and the moment it sees a difference it re-applies the Git-declared manifest, no human decision required. Git still says `replicas: 5`. The on-call engineer's `kubectl scale` creates drift the instant it runs, and on ArgoCD's next reconciliation pass -- every few minutes by default, which lines up exactly with the roughly-three-minute pattern described -- the agent sees `live != desired` and reverts the live state straight back down to match Git. Rerunning the scale command just restarts the same cycle, because it never changes what Git says, and Git is what the reconciler treats as authoritative.

The correct fix is to stop fighting the reconciler and instead change the thing it's enforcing: commit the real capacity change to Git. That means opening a PR that bumps `replicas` in the relevant overlay (or, better, replacing a static replica count with an HPA if the actual need is to handle variable traffic rather than a permanent step up) and letting ArgoCD apply that change through its normal sync, the same promotion mechanism used for any other config change. Once Git says `replicas: 10` (or the HPA is in place), the reconciler stops reverting it, because there's no longer a disagreement between live state and desired state -- selfHeal is still fully active and still protecting every other resource from drift, it's just no longer working against this one.

What I would not do is turn off `selfHeal` cluster-wide or on this `Application` to make the symptom go away -- that reopens drift risk for every resource under that `Application`, not just this one, and defeats the entire reason GitOps makes Git a trustworthy source of truth in the first place. During an incident specifically, the right instinct is 'commit the real fix now,' not 'repeatedly out-run the reconciler with manual edits.'
questions.professionalAnswer:
First thing I'd tell the team is: nothing's broken here, ArgoCD is working exactly as designed, and that's actually the useful framing to lead with because it stops people from chasing a phantom bug. Somewhere on that `Application`, `selfHeal` is set to true, which means ArgoCD is sitting there every few minutes comparing what's live against what Git says, and Git still says five replicas. So every time on-call bumps it to ten by hand, they're creating drift, and a few minutes later the reconciler just quietly puts it back, because as far as ArgoCD's concerned, the cluster disagreeing with Git is the bug, not the manual scale.

What I'd actually do -- and I'd say this to the on-call engineer directly in the moment -- is stop re-running `kubectl scale` and instead just open the PR. Bump replicas in the overlay, or honestly if traffic's genuinely variable I'd rather put an HPA in there instead of a static number, and let ArgoCD apply that like it would any other config change. That ends the fight immediately because now Git and the cluster agree.

The one thing I'd push back on hard if someone suggested it: don't turn off selfHeal to make this go away. That's the knob that's quietly protecting every other resource under that Application from the exact same kind of drift, and turning it off cluster-wide to solve a one-resource problem trades a minor annoyance for a much bigger risk.
questions.example:
# the actual fix -- a PR against the overlay, not another kubectl command
# overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml
patches:
  - target:
      kind: Deployment
      name: payments-api
    patch: |-
      - op: replace
        path: /spec/replicas
        value: 10

# or, better for variable traffic -- an HPA committed alongside the Deployment
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: payments-api
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: payments-api
  minReplicas: 5
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 70
commonMistakes: Assuming the reverted replica count is a bug or a flaky controller rather than selfHeal working as designed
Repeatedly re-running kubectl scale instead of committing the change to Git
Disabling selfHeal cluster-wide or on the whole Application as a quick fix, reopening drift risk everywhere
Not distinguishing an 'alert only' sync policy from a 'selfHeal: true' one when diagnosing the behavior
Editing the base manifest instead of the environment-specific overlay for what is an environment-specific capacity need
Defaulting to a static replica bump when an HPA is the more correct long-term fix for variable traffic
keyPoints: selfHeal: true makes ArgoCD revert any manual drift on its next reconciliation pass
The reconciliation loop runs every few minutes by default, matching the observed ~3-minute pattern
Git still says replicas: 5, so per the single-source-of-truth model, Git wins
The correct fix is committing the desired state to Git via a PR, not repeated kubectl edits
Disabling selfHeal fleet-wide to work around one incident reopens drift risk everywhere, not just here
An HPA may be the more appropriate long-term fix than a static replica bump for variable traffic

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies selfHeal: true as the mechanism reverting the manual change
Explains why the ~3-minute pattern matches the reconciliation loop interval
Prescribes committing the fix to Git as the correct resolution
Explicitly rejects disabling selfHeal as the fix, with reasoning
Considers a more durable fix (e.g. HPA) where relevant
