questions.title: Navigating the Real Tension Between Reliability and Feature Velocity
questions.prompt: Describe a time you had to push back on feature work -- or had to defend a team's right to ship riskier work -- because of a reliability constraint. How did you frame that conversation, and what made it a decision based on data rather than a political argument? If this hasn't come up directly for you, explain how you'd use an error budget to resolve this tension in practice, including what you would actually do differently when a team is burning its budget too fast versus when it has budget to spare.
questions.modelAnswer:
The competition between reliability work and feature work is structural, not a matter of attitude or who cares more about quality. Every hour an engineer spends hardening a retry path or chasing a flaky dependency is an hour not spent shipping the next feature, because a team has a fixed number of engineering hours and both kinds of work draw from the same pool. Pretending that tension doesn't exist, or resolving it by fiat ('just do both'), doesn't remove the tradeoff -- it just means the tradeoff gets made implicitly and inconsistently, usually in favor of whichever pressure is loudest that week.

An error budget is what turns that competition into a quantified, negotiated tradeoff instead of a recurring political argument. If a service's SLO is 99.9% availability over 30 days, the error budget is the 0.1% of allowed unreliability -- a concrete, spendable quantity both sides agreed to in advance. As long as the team is operating inside that budget, they have an explicit, data-backed license to take risks: ship faster, run experiments, defer some hardening work, because the data shows they can afford it.

When a team is burning that budget too fast, it isn't a crisis to be managed quietly in the moment -- it's a pre-agreed trigger. Feature launches that would add risk get paused, and the next sprint's priority shifts toward the reliability work actually causing the burn. That isn't punishment; it's the system working exactly as designed, because everyone agreed in advance what 'spent too fast' means and what happens next. Teams that track the error budget but never actually let it stop a launch have the dashboard without the practice, and they rediscover the tension the hard way during the next outage.

The flip side matters just as much and gets ignored more often: a team sitting comfortably inside its error budget has real, data-backed permission to take more risk, not just a passive pat on the back. That's an active decision -- greenlighting a riskier launch, deprioritizing a reliability investment the data says isn't needed yet, reallocating that freed-up time toward features. Treating a healthy budget as something to just bank quietly, instead of a signal to actually ship faster, wastes the other half of what the mechanism is for.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd frame it for the team like this: this isn't about who's being reckless or who's too cautious, it's that we only have so many engineering hours, and reliability work and feature work are both drawing from the same pool. If we don't make that tradeoff explicit, it just gets decided by whoever's shouting loudest that week, which is a bad way to run things.

What I actually did was point to the error budget instead of making a personal judgment call. The service had a 99.9% SLO, so there's a real, spendable 0.1% budget, and when a product team wanted to push a risky launch while we were deep into burning that budget on an unrelated issue, I didn't argue about whether they were being reckless -- I pointed at the number we'd all already agreed to respect, and said the budget says we pause, not me. That's the part that keeps it from turning into a political fight -- nobody has to win an argument, the pre-agreed number already answered the question.

And I'd be honest that the part people usually get wrong is only paying attention when the budget's nearly gone. When a team has budget to spare, that's also a real decision point -- I'd actively tell a team 'you've got room, let's greenlight that riskier launch, or let's pull that hardening work off the roadmap for now and put the time into features,' instead of just quietly letting the surplus sit there unused. The whole mechanism only works if both directions actually happen -- pausing when you're burning too fast, and actually spending the surplus when you have it -- otherwise you've just got a dashboard nobody's really using.
commonMistakes: Treating the reliability-vs-velocity conflict as a personality or culture problem instead of a structural capacity tradeoff
Resolving the tension by fiat ('just do both') instead of with a quantified budget both sides agreed to in advance
Tracking error budget burn but never actually letting it pause a risky launch -- the dashboard without the practice
Only acting when the budget is nearly exhausted and ignoring the surplus case as a real, active decision
Framing the pushback as a personal judgment call rather than pointing to the pre-agreed number and policy
Treating a budget-triggered pause as a punishment to apologize for instead of the system working as designed
keyPoints: The competition for engineering time between reliability work and feature work is structural, not a matter of attitude
An error budget (100% minus the SLO) is a concrete, spendable quantity both sides agreed to in advance
Operating inside budget is explicit, data-backed license to take risk and ship faster
Burning budget too fast is a pre-agreed trigger: pause risky launches, reprioritize toward the reliability work causing the burn
That pause is the system working as designed, not a punishment negotiated in the moment
A budget surplus is also an active decision -- ship faster or deprioritize unneeded reliability work, not just a thing to note
Tracking burn without ever letting it block a launch is the dashboard without the practice

Explains the error budget mechanism as a pre-agreed, quantified, negotiated tradeoff
Correctly describes what actually happens when budget burns too fast (concrete pause/reprioritization)
Correctly describes what a budget surplus licenses, as an active decision
Answer is grounded in a specific, credible example or concrete practice rather than platitudes
